Śrīḥ!
The *Prāṇatoṣiṇī* was composed by Śrī Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya,
having compiled it from the Tantric scriptures.
It was published by the venerable Śrī Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācāryya, a learned family head and holder of the title of Upādhyāya,
in the city of Calcutta.
Printed at the Calcutta Press.
5) Having bowed to the lotus feet of the beloved [deity], which bestow the fruits of the four aims of human life, [this] section on devotion...
Rāmatoṣaṇa composes the fifth section on devotion (*bhaktikāṇḍa*).
Now, the glossary (*nirghaṇṭa*) of this fifth section on devotion is being stated:
first, the morning rites; thereafter, [the worship] of Gaṇeśa, followed by bathing and so forth.
Furthermore, the specific details of the *tarpaṇa* (libation) and its fruit follow thereafter.

[The procedure includes] performing the *nyāsa* of Śrī Gaṇeśa, the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), and the *mātṛkā-nyāsa*; the censure of actions that ought not to be done; and the *ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa*.
Immediately following that is the method for the rite of Mātṛkā-nyāsa;
then another nyāsa, followed by meditation (dhyāna) and the construction of the yantra.
Then there is the worship of the pedestal (pīṭha-pūjā) and so forth, the invocation (āvāhana), and finally the sequence of worship (pūjā-krama).
The eightfold offering of scents for Gaṇeśa, followed by flowers; then the varieties of incense, lamps, and so forth, and thereafter the worship of the deities of the enclosure (āvaraṇārccā);
then the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) of Gaṇeśa, and after that, rites for specific desires (kāmyakarma).
Immediately following that is the *sādhana* of Mahālakṣmī and others;
thereafter, the *gaṇeśa-mantra* and the *yantra* suitable for wearing;
after that, rites such as attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), and then further meditations.
The distinction of castes according to the distinction of karma; the three seed-syllables of Gaṇeśvara;
then another meditation; then the mudrā; then another preliminary rite (puraścaryā);
then the meditation on the powers such as the intense (tīvra) and others; and after that, the mantra of the sacred seat (pīṭha).
The supreme worship consists of the worship of the retinue and the worship of the eight-armed one;
then follows the worship of the Mouse, the origin of the Gaṇapati of Turmeric,
the Gaṇeśa Upaniṣad, and thereafter the hymn to the Lord of Gaṇas.
The armor-mantra of Gaṇanātha was produced by Lipilambodara;
other [mantras] as well are to be understood by the learned after observing them in their proper places. Thus is stated the conclusion of the first chapter.
The Bāṇaliṅga, its classification, its identifying marks, and its examination;
the etymology of the word "Bāṇa," the praise of the Bāṇaliṅga,
the fruit of its worship, and thereafter the fruit of its installation.
The *rasaliṅga* fruit, and thereafter the censurable *liṅga*;
the auspicious *liṅga*, the *vāṇaliṅga*, and then the cause of its manifestation;
the site of the *vāṇaliṅga*, and the *vāṇaliṅga* itself of many varieties.
Meditation, worship, and praise, as well as the characteristics of the *raudra-liṅga* and other types, follow from that;

the fruit of worshipping a *liṅga* made of stone is superior to one produced from clay and other materials. Immediately after that is the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of a *liṅga* made of metal and other substances.
The fruit of worshipping a *liṅga* with power (*śakti*) is established by its respective authorities;
for the different castes beginning with the Brahmin, the fruit of clay is gross, while that arising from stone and other materials is more subtle.
Furthermore, the very manifestation of the *liṅga* according to the five threads (*pañcasūtra*) and so forth is what bestows the fruit.
Immediately thereafter [is described] the fruit of the greatness of the *liṅga* and its worship;
then follows the greatness of the *rasaliṅga*, the fashioning of that *liṅga*,
the origin of the *liṅga* such as the Vaiṣṇava and others, and the eligibility for the worship of the *liṅga*.
In passages concerning the censure of not doing that [worship] and so forth,
there is the origin of the Śiva-liṅga and the eligibility of Vaiṣṇavas and others for the worship of the liṅga;
in passages concerning the censure of not performing that and so forth, there is the injunction for the ritual worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
"The fruit of installing the *liṅga*, followed by optional worship (*kāmyapūjā*)—
this is declared to be the conclusion of the second chapter.
Clay from sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*) and other locations should be taken for the rite of fashioning the Śiva-image."
The river, minor characteristics, and the measurement of the linga;
the mantra for preparing the clay, and the censure for ignorance of the mantra;
the mantra for the construction, its dimensions, the consecration, and the ritual placement (nyāsa).
Then comes breath control (prāṇāyāma), followed by meditation (dhyāna); after that, the invocation (āvāhana).
Then follows the six-syllable mantra (ṣaḍakṣara), worship (pūjā), and the worship of the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti).
Next is the recitation (japa), the offering of it (samarpaṇa), the playing of musical instruments, and finally, prostration (nati).
Then follows the dismissal (*visarjana*), after which comes the worship (*pūjā*) and the sacred thread (*sūtra*).
Next is the station of the worshipper (*pūjakasthāna*), followed by defects due to deficiency or excess.
Then, before all else, is the worship of the *liṅga*; otherwise, there is a defect.
Then follows the offering of flowers and the majesty of the flower itself;
the majesty of the *vijayā* leaf, the procedure for worshipping the *kāmya-liṅga*,
the daily worship of the *liṅga*, and thereafter the fruit offered to the *liṅga*.

The fruit of worshipping a *liṅga* for a single day is the pacification of misfortune (*riṣṭaśānti*). Worship that fulfills all desires is superior; therefore, what is offered to the *liṅga* is not to be taken back. That which is placed in a vessel at that time—the food offering (*naivedya*)—is the most excellent thing to be consumed.
The fault in taking Śiva’s own property and its specific expiation;
the acceptance of offerings presented to a Bāṇaliṅga as well as those presented to a self-manifested (svayambhū) linga;
and the determination regarding the materials of the *nirmālya*—all this is likewise recorded in the traditions of the Ṛṣis and others.
Then follows the Pāśupata weapon [mantra], followed by the hymn to the Liṅga;
thereafter the armor (kavaca) of Śiva, then the majesty of the bilva tree and so forth,
then the majesty of the rudrākṣa, and immediately after that the section on consciousness (saṃvit).
Having thus determined that this is the completion of the third section,
[I have described] the origin of the Śālagrāma stone, the cause of the discus-mark,
the lack of effort regarding it, the acquisition of the Viṣṇu-stone, and the supreme fruit resulting therefrom.
The qualities and defects such as smoothness and so forth; the determination of defects regarding one who has desires;
the fruit arising from the worship of the twelve discs of the Śālagrāma;
the fruit according to the number of discs; and the description of the Śālagrāma.
The fruit of residing at Śālagrāma is described, followed by its various classifications;

thereafter follows the specific distinctions of the discus-mark according to the classes of Brahmins and others; and subsequently, the prohibition against touching or worshipping [the marks] by those of the royal (Kṣatriya) and other castes is set forth.
Even for the sake of food, one must not perform the worship of the Śālagrāma without [proper ritual];
likewise, neither a pair of discs nor a pair of lingas should ever be worshipped in the home.
The fruit of worshipping twelve or more discs is lost through the sale of a disc.
There shall be no fault, and immediately thereafter follows the fruit of worshipping the discus; next is the fruit of the confluence of the Gaṇḍakī and the Dvārakā-cakra;
and beyond that, the fruit of the worship of Viṣṇu at Śālagrāma is to be known.
The completion of the fourth chapter has been declared;
thereafter follow the marks of the wheels at Dvārakā, its greatness,
and subsequently the auspicious and inauspicious results according to the specific colors thereof.
First is the breaking of the stone disc, then the difference in names;
thereafter are the rites such as the restoration of ruined temples, followed by the worship of the Śālagrāma stone. Then follows the Ṣaṭpadī hymn, prostration, and finally the prayer.

Drinking the nectar of his feet and bearing it upon one’s head; not drinking [that water] yet bearing it on the head; disparaging the water from the feet of a brāhmaṇa; the rite of offering the food (naivedya); the mantra; and the manual for worship (arcana-sūtra).
Then follow the mantras for the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*), and thereafter the rites for desired results (*kāmyakarman*).
After that, the majesty of the name of Śrī Viṣṇu, and then the hundred names.
Following that, [it is taught that] worship of Viṣṇu using wooden vessels and the like brings about defects.
Worship performed in vessels of gold and other precious materials yields fruit beyond measure;
thereafter follows the majesty of the Puruṣasūkta, the threefold fruit of ritual bathing,
the fruit of fragrant unguents for the bath, and the auspicious and inauspicious results concerning the conch.
The characteristics of the Tripadī, the greatness of Tulasī and so forth, the wearing of the garland, the praise of the Vaiṣṇava,
and the section on the lunar days of the ten incarnations constitute the fifth chapter here.
Then follows the determination of the Mahāvidyās and the proclamation of their majesty;
after that, Bhairava [is described],
followed by the determination of Mahārātri and the others, and thereafter the origin of the Vidyās.
(590) The nature of Mahākālī, the description of the *ālīḍha* posture and so forth, asceticism (*tapas*), the praise of the Kālī mantra, the fault of disparaging the first [mantra],
the two Kālī mantras, and the pacification (*śānti*) and other rites performed with those two.
The fruit of the two mantras, as well as the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the sages and other factors,
the tantric rites such as restraint (saṃyama), and the duties to be performed by the Guru—
whether by his sons and others, or by himself, but never through another— [must be carried out].
This is the determination of the fruit for one who has performed the rites prescribed in the Tantras by a Guru.

When the rite is performed for the wife of the Guru, no fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed here. There is censure regarding that rite when it is performed according to the ordinances of a domestic priest (purohita).
The prohibition of worship in the presence of others has been proclaimed;
alternatively, the worship prescribed in the Vaiṣṇava tantras is ordained there.
Furthermore, devotion elsewhere [than to one's own] chosen deity, as well as its disparagement, is likewise forbidden.
And worship is threefold; beyond that is the fruit of external worship.
Then follows the Sūtra of Worship, and likewise the Sūtra of Concise Worship.
Also included are the ritual procedure for daily worship and the preliminary practice of the two mantras.
Then follows the hymn of one hundred names and the hymn of praise to Mahāvidyā;
then the armor (kavaca) of Mahāvidyā and the armor of Kālī;
thereafter, the praise of the Śāktas and the reason for the Śākta nature of the Brahmins.
The prohibition of other forms of worship for one who is devoted to the worship of Śakti is [stated];
other matters as well should be understood by the wise according to their proper place.
Thus is declared the conclusion of the sixth chapter.
The determination of the names of the *kumārī* according to the distinctions of age, such as one year and so forth;
the specific details therein according to various *tantras*;
the location for the worship of the *kumārī*, its fruit, and the determination of the appropriate time for it.
Whatever fruit there is from giving flowers and other offerings, as well as food,
that is the place of worship;
thereafter, Manu [states] the sequence of worship for the maidens, followed by prostration.

Then follows the giving of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and so forth, the fruit of the maiden’s marriage, the fruit of the wedding ceremony itself, the preliminary consecration (*puraskriyā*) of its mantra,
and immediately thereafter, the ritual application (*prayoga*) for the worship of the virgin (*kumārikā*).
Then follows the *Kumārīstavarāja* and the *Kumārīkavaca*,
the praise of the Brāhmaṇa, the fruit arising from the livelihood of a teacher,
the fruit of a Brāhmaṇa’s curse, and after that, the pilgrimage to sacred fords (*tīrthayātrā*).
The determination of prohibited seats during travel in specific directions;
the determination of the Yoginīs according to specific lunar days (tithis) and astrological conjunctions (yogas);
and likewise, the prohibition of travel during a yoga resulting from the combination of a lunar day and a lunar mansion (nakṣatra).

(p. 591) Next follows the prohibition regarding the birth month and so forth, and the determination of the [auspicious] time such as dawn; then, travel in specific directions for one facing a particular direction;
and therein, the determination of the specific materials required for the journey.
The determination regarding Gayā, the description of the Preta-śilā,
the ascertainment of the Golaka-liṅga and others, the offering of one's own piṇḍas,
the fruit thereof as told by Agastya, and the determination of the proper time for one's own rites.
In that regard, there is no fixed rule for the timing of the *śrāddha* rite.
When performing a *śrāddha* at the equinox (*viṣuva*), there is a prohibition against meat;
furthermore, in the case of a *śrāddha* with raw food (*āma-śrāddha*), there is a prohibition against raw meat.
When a śrāddha with meat has been performed, there is censure regarding the consumption of meatless food;
likewise, there is a rule for the offering of meat during annual śrāddhas and similar rites.
Conversely, when a meatless śrāddha has been performed, there is a fault in eating meat.
Next follows the censure of a Brahmin’s eating when invited by a Śūdra;
then the meat that should be given at a Śrāddha and its fruit;
then the meat that should be avoided, as well as the fish that should be offered and likewise those that should be avoided.
Immediately following that is the prohibition against incense, ripe plantains, and similar items;
then the determination of the specific vessels, the foods, the satisfaction [of ancestors], and the duration of time in the *śrāddha* rite;
as well as the invitation, the departure [of guests], and the majesty of Kāśī itself.
Thus, the conclusion of the seventh section has been recounted by me.
This section on devotion, consisting of seven chapters and endowed with fruits,
is that for the sake of which gods, humans, kinnaras, and others performed fierce austerities.

O wise ones! May you not mock me for this, for I have discharged an incomparable and terrible arrow with such haste that it struck a falling leaf; such is the miserable plight of one who creates obstacles for others.

May they behold repeatedly this Lord, who is free from desire, the all-pervading one who assumes various forms through the qualities of māyā that are difficult to abandon, yet whose mind is always possessed by the notions of "you" and "I."
Now begins the section on Gaṇeśa.
In the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*, which is the commentary on the second section (*kāṇḍa*) held within the *Kulamūlāvatārakalpasūtraṭīkā*.

Having risen during the *muhūrta* sacred to Brahmā, one should again remember one’s own guru seated upon a white lotus on the crown of the head— white in complexion, with two eyes and a peaceful countenance, his hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having prostrated according to the rule and gone outside, the practitioner, having performed the necessary purifications, cleansing, sipping water, brushing his teeth,
washing his face, and so forth, should perform his bath.
Having invoked the sacred ford from the solar disc by means of the heart-mantra and the goad-mantra,
and having united it with the lunar, solar, and fiery mandalas within the water,
the practitioner, being well-composed, should contemplate this and immerse himself in its midst.
Having begun with the root mantra and recited it three times mentally, he should rise up, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and empower his body with the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga). Then,
by means of the root mantra and the mudrā known as the "water-pot" (kalaśa), he should consecrate himself.
Then, having consecrated water seven times with the mantra and drunk it,
he should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana), put on two clean garments,
sip water again, and perform the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa) as before.
One should perform a sevenfold sprinkling with drops of water falling from the hand held downward in the left, while reciting the root mantra; then,
having placed the remaining water in the right hand, it should be consecrated with the mantra.
Standing, one should offer three handfuls of *arghya* water to the Sun with the *Gāyatrī* mantra.
Likewise: "I shall now describe the fourfold libation (*tarpaṇa*) which grants all desired objects."
In a solitary, secluded forest, free from all disturbances,
the mantra-practitioner, having performed his ablutions and other rites, and being endowed with the ritual placements (nyāsa) as before,
should visualize a blossoming lotus grove in the middle of the lake.
In its center, one should meditate upon a great lotus, resembling the rising sun,
lofty, rich in fragrance, delightful, and captivating; it is fully blossomed,
or else one who possesses a flood of purity may visualize it as such.

Having established an auspicious seat made of gold or other precious materials— or, according to one's means, a new vessel of clay— wide and with a very large mouth, using water from rivers, streams, or ponds;
Having filled it with pure water, one should visualize a lotus there; then,
having ascertained oneself as Gaṇanāyaka, one should approach him by means of a row of silver steps from the center of that lotus.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśāna, who is seated and adorned with all ornaments,
with handfuls of fragrant flowers as before;

Having placed [the gaze] at the tip of the nose above the head of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), and having clearly visualized his body as being filled by a stream of nectar, one should meditate upon the head of Gaṇeśa with waters moistened by moon-essence, sandalwood, saffron, and musk.
First, having gratified [the deities] four times with the root mantra, one should likewise offer four oblations each to the Couple, the Six Gaṇeśas, and the two Treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma,
using their respective seed-syllables and other components, ending with *svāhā*.
The wise practitioner should offer libations with the root mantra preceded by four repetitions;
having performed this one hundred and eight times in total, this is considered the "lesser" (kaniṣṭha) sequence.
Alternatively, the knower of distinctions may offer libations with the root mantra eight times.
One should satisfy [the deities] beginning with Śrī and ending with Nidhi, individually and separately,
by dividing them into four cycles preceded by the root mantra.
Thus, this middle sequence consists of two hundred and sixteen [recitations].
Alternatively, having first offered libations twenty times with the root mantra,
one should offer four times each with the individual syllables of the mantra followed by *svāhā*,
and then, as before, offer four times with the root mantra.
After the sacrifice of the *mithuna* (couple) and others, one should perform the libation as before.
Taken together, there would be four hundred and forty-four [offerings].
This is declared to be the sequence of the "Elder" (*jyeṣṭha*) by those who know reality and are learned in the Tantras.
Having thus bathed the body [of the deity] with waters consisting of nectar,
and having again gratified the God with perfumes and other offerings, one who knows the proper place and time should pray for whatever is most desired, offer salutations, and then depart.
Thus, the practitioner who daily gratifies [the deities] at the beginning of the day will certainly obtain all desired objects from the mandala without any obstacle.
Also in the thirteenth chapter of the Śāradātilaka:
A man, remaining unwearied, should satisfy the Sun and Gaṇanāyaka with pure waters four hundred and forty-four times;
before the [completion of the] maṇḍala, he shall obtain his desired goal in abundance.
In the ritual of satiation (tarpaṇa), however, this is the specific distinction for all mantras:
Having descended from playing upon the peak of the golden Mount Udaya, he arrives at the golden steps and receives abundant alms consisting of lotuses and other offerings.

Having eaten with a joyful mind, one should worship the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnapa) as before; thus he is remembered [to be honored] at dawn. Likewise, having satisfied him with offerings of jasmine flowers (śaśikalāklāma), the procedure for the libation (tarpaṇa) is: "Gaṃ, I satisfy Gaṇeśa."

Gradually, "four hundred" means that such an oblation is performed with four substances on each lunar day (*tithi*). [This is prescribed] in the event of drought, during terrible fear, when there is affliction from kings, thieves, and the like, in great battle, in dispute, and in the crisis of extreme poverty.
In all rites such as marriage and especially in all matters of desire,
one with a tranquil mind should perform propitiation in this manner through mental offerings;
by the power of Śrī Gaṇeśa, everything is accomplished effortlessly.
With an undisturbed mind, the practitioner should meditate upon an ocean of sugarcane juice.
In its midst is the island of coral, resembling the rising sun;
in the center of that is a great ground made of divine Jāmbūnada gold.
Above that, in the Kalpako garden, there is a vast ground made of jewels,
frequented by gentle breezes and reddened by the light of moonbeams;
in its center is a divine pavilion, resplendent with pillars of precious gems.
It was beautifully smeared with thick vermilion paste, enchanting,
enriched with canopies of pearls and gems, adorned with flower garlands,
and most captivating, radiant with bells, banners, and streamers.
Having reflected thus, [he beheld] that [tree] which was perpetually and simultaneously worshipped by hosts of gods in its midst, attended by the six seasons beginning with spring,
and enriched with jewels, gems, and coral, as well as fruits, blossoms, and sprouts.

One should meditate upon the great wish-fulfilling tree (kalpataru), which is adorned and bestows all fruits. At the root of that wish-fulfilling tree is a great lion-throne composed of the nine jewels; in its center is a radiant pericarp with six corners.
The knower of mantras, best among his peers, should meditate upon this lotus as the script.
This is the section on the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to the prescribed rule:
with the heel of the right foot pressing upon the base of the penis below the anus,
keeping the body, head, and neck erect, and having the senses and mind restrained.
With his hands joined at the heart and his eyes fixed on the tip of the nose,
he should contemplate the pervasive power (vyāpinī-śakti) extending from the big toe to the crown of the head, filling the entire hollow interior of his body both within and without.
Restraining the former vital breaths, the mind, the individual soul, and the ego along with the sense of "I," the wise one should lead them from the *mūlādhāra* by the path taught by the Guru;
having awakened the power of Kuṇḍalinī, he should lead both himself and [the others] together with her.
Having unified [the breath] with the weapon-mantra through the sequence of dissolving the knots,
one should worship for half [the duration] while experiencing supreme bliss through the *haṃsa* during the retention (*kumbhaka*) and exhalation (*udvāta*).
With undistracted mind, having drawn the individual soul (jīvātman) from the head through the central path of Suṣumṇā and having united it with Śiva residing at the end of the twelve,
one should contemplate the elements and the phonemes as dissolved.
Having meditated upon the smoky-colored seed-syllable of fire (Ra) with its bindu at the navel,
one should dry up the body by means of the *haṃsa* and the fierce wind.
Then, by means of five upward thrusts (*udghāta*), [one should draw it] to the lotus of the heart-lake.
Having visualized within a hexagon Narasiṃha, filled with garlands of flames arising from his seed-syllables,
one should contemplate the substrate— the stainless and healthy price—
as being consumed by the flame of that seed-syllable and reduced to ashes.
Having thoroughly dispersed that entire heap of ashes by means of the wind arising from the seed-syllable of fire (RAṂ),

one should thereafter, with self-restraint, [place it] within the consciousness through the path of emanation, starting from the principles (tattvas) and so forth produced from Śiva and Śakti, using the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having produced the body, which is a great illusion in the form of radiant energy,
one should contemplate the water-seed situated within the seed-syllable of the moon of consciousness (*cic-candra*).
Within the ocean of nectar arisen from that [water-seed], one should imagine a great bubble.
Then one should contemplate the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) situated within the midst of the bubble;
therein, having meditated upon the universe and then upon the Goddess in the lotus of her heart,
one should withdraw one's own consciousness from the sky of consciousness through the realization "I am That."
Then, one should contemplate the self as perfectly stable by means of the seed-syllable *bhūḥ*.
Having again flooded the body, both external and internal, with nectar,
the wise one should mentally visualize the Śakti returned to her own place.
Having thus performed the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should again perform the ritual placement (nyāsa).
The placement of the *mātṛkā* (the alphabet) is also described in that very same place.

One should know that any recitation or other rite performed for all mantras without the placement of the letters [of the alphabet] is fruitless; therefore, one should first place the alphabet. [This is done] with the twelve initial vowels, beginning with *a*, along with the nasals (*ṣaṇḍavarya*) and the visarga.

The mantra-practitioner should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅgaka*) using the six groups of consonants beginning with *ka*, enclosed [by vowels]. He should place the vowels at the hairline, the perimeter of the face, the two eyes, the two ears,
and in the pairs consisting of the nose, cheeks, lips, and teeth, as well as on the crown of the head and the mouth.
One should place the five consonants of the *ca*-group on the two arms and the joints of the feet;
the *ya*-group on the two sides, the back, the navel, and the heart, respectively.
One should place the *ya*-group and the others upon the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), according to the sequence of the self by means of the self.
Having thus performed the placement of the Mātṛkā, one should thereafter perform the placement in this manner:
having thus placed the Mātṛkā, the self-controlled practitioner should subsequently place [the letters] five times with the root mantra upon the locations that will be described hereafter.
Having placed the six seed-syllables (*bīja*) in sequence upon the crown, face, heart, secret place, feet, and heart,
one should cause the remaining mantra-syllables to pervade the entire body.
One should then place [the syllables] on the head, forehead, eyes, mouth, crest-lock, and tongue.
The six seed-syllables are placed in the mouth by the preceptor with mantras throughout the entire body:
on the head, between the eyebrows, in the middle of the forehead, in the two ears, in the pair of eyes and nostrils,
in the mouth, in the two hands and feet, and in the four radiant joints.
One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) with the syllables of the mantra upon the camphor-like heart-lotus and the body;
likewise, one should separately place the five pairs (*mithuna*) upon the head, face, heart-lotus, secret place, and feet,
using their respective seed-syllables and names.
The teachers Īśānaśiva, who know the truth of all the scriptures,
have declared the fifth [pair] to be Mithuna and the sixth to be Kamala. Then, one should perform the placement of the six root-aṅgas according to the prescribed measure.
By means of the six seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the [mantras] beginning with *Āgama*, conjoined with the fire-mantra (*vahni*),
the birth (*utpatti*) of celibate students (*brahmacārin*) occurs from the thumb to the little finger;
for householders (*gṛhastha*), their maintenance (*sthiti*) occurs from the middle finger to the index finger.

For ascetics, the withdrawal [of the fingers] should begin from the little finger and end at the thumb; the practitioner of mantra, according to his stage of life (āśrama), should perform this for both hands,
as well as upon the fingers including the tips, the palms, and the backs.
Having performed the placement [of mantras], one should assign them to the heart and other parts by means of the mudrās of the heart and so forth.
Likewise: on the head, the eyes, the tongue, the heart, the navel, the crown of the head, and the knees.
One should place Vināyaka and the other lords of obstacles at the tips of the feet. [These are:
Vināyaka, Virūpākṣa, Krūrakarman, Aparājita, Caṇḍavega, Hayagrīva, Karāla, and Caṇḍavikrama.
Likewise, the best of practitioners should place [the mantras] upon those very parts including the neck:
Vighna, Vināyaka, Vīra, Śūra, and Vadana.
Then Gajavaktra, after that Ekadanta,
then Lambodara, Kṣipra, and Mahāgaṇapa;
likewise the Mothers beginning with Brahmāṇī, and the Bhairavas beginning with Asitāṅga.
One should place the eight [syllables] beginning with the seed-syllable of Śakti in their respective locations:
on the forehead, the two arms, the two breasts, the two sides, the abdomen,
the right side, the right throat, the back of the neck, and the heart, in due order.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), one should, with a concentrated mind,
perform meditation [on the Lord] whose sides are embraced by the Fortune of Success (Siddhilakṣmī), who bears the crescent moon as his crest-ornament,
who is of a deep red hue, and who holds a citron, a mace, a lotus, a sugarcane bow, and a conch.

[I salute] Vighneśvara, who holds in his eleven hands— like those of Indra— a trident, the Sudarśana discus, a conch, a blue lotus, a cluster of grain, his own teeth, and a jeweled bell; whose temples are flowing with rut, who is full of bliss, and who effects the destruction of all obstacles.
Some say one should meditate on the ten-armed [form].
Now I shall explain the meditation according to pervasion, the world, and the body:
the syllable *kṣmā* is in the three void-bodies, and the syllable *pavana* is in the belly.
He whose eyes are the sun, moon, and fire; whose two ears are the ten directions;
who has the primordial matter (pradhāna) as his head; the Lord of Beings, whose activity is the faculty of intellect (buddhi);
the divine, beginningless and endless mass of splendor, free from all ailment.
One should meditate upon the Lord Gaṇeśāna, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss.
Having thus explained this pervasiveness, the meditation on the embodied form is now described.
With an undisturbed mind, the practitioner of mantra should contemplate the ocean of sugarcane juice.
Therein, seated in the center, is the elephant-faced one,
three-eyed, with a single tusk, ten arms, a conch-like neck, and a large belly;
his right foot rests upon a lotus, while his middle lotus-foot hangs down.
Resembling the rising sun, clothed in yellow garments,
with matted locks as red as the twilight and adorned with golden ornaments,
he has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament and wears a serpent as his sacred thread.
His broad and noble chest was radiant with the brilliance of a multitude of gems;
he was adorned with jewels, pearls, corals, and other ornaments, as well as a girdle around his waist;
and he shone with his left calf bound by a garland of tinkling bells.
Beginning from the lower right hand, with a downward-hanging stream [of light],
he holds in his right arms a mace, a trident, a staff, a sword, and a horn;
and in [the others] a rice-ear, a noose, a discus, a cluster of sugarcane, and a citron.

Others know [the Lord] as holding a citron, a mace, a bow of sugarcane, a trident, and the Sudarśana discus; and in His left hands, a lotus, a noose, a stone, rice-grains, and a tusk. He wears ornaments on His limbs, and His lotus-feet are resplendent with anklets.
He is embraced by Śakti, who rests upon his left side, is adorned with all ornaments,
and holds a lotus in her hand; he bestows the face of all sovereignty,
having playfully placed a jeweled pitcher upon the tip of his trunk.
He constantly showers the practitioner on all sides with rains of jewels;
he drives away the bees greedy for rut-fluid by the flapping of his ears;
and he is perpetually attended by gods and asuras.
"With his mind filled with hymns of praise raised with heroic shouts, the best of practitioners, having meditated upon the Lord Mahāgaṇeśāna... Thus it is said;
the method for constructing the yantra for this [mantra] is also found in that very same place.
Having drawn [the design] with *kusoda* paste, water, musk, camphor, sandalwood, and saffron,
or else having written it with a golden needle or with a blade of *dūrvā* grass,
the wise man should draw a lotus, beautiful and with perfectly even lines.
The wise practitioner should place [the image] upon a golden pedestal; in its absence, on one made of śrīparṇī wood, or on a well-constructed square base.
Having first worshipped the Guru and Gaṇeśvara on his left and right sides respectively, he should proceed.
Having obtained their permission, one should commence the worship of the sacred seats (pīṭha-pūjā).

Having worshipped, in successive order from top to bottom, the Support-Energy (Ādhāraśakti), Ananta, and the Earth like a tortoise, one should thereafter worship [the deities] in the directions starting with the intermediate ones.
One should worship the lion-throne with the mantras in due order:
"The foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), seated and adorned with white ornaments, white in appearance, should be meditated upon; by the command of Śiva, she sustains the worlds."
In this context, through the thirty-two principles beginning with Earth and ending with Vidyā,
which take the form of sacred seats (pīṭha), Ananta becomes the one described as the "Anantāsana" (the seat of Ananta).
Likewise: "Dharma, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty—this tetrad is the 'tetrad on the lion-throne seat'. (p. 598)
The commentary on the Kalpasūtra-Ṭīkā:

In all four legs, beginning with the southeast (āgneya) and so forth, the four [principles] beginning with Adharma are situated respectively; and in the four directions beginning with the east, the same four are located in order.

Dharma is red and bull-shaped; Jñāna is a lion and dark blue; Vairāgya has the form of a ghost and is white; Aiśvarya is lunar-white. These lords, beginning with Dharma, are seated in order upon a pedestal of gold and jewels.
Likewise:
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are upon that lotus-throne;
and Māyā, in the form of a trident, whose nature is concealed as Vidyā.
The practitioner of mantra should worship the lotus of the letters, which bestows ever-increasing bliss;
in its center, he should worship the three mandalas:
subsequently, the solar mandala on the petals and the lunar mandala in the pericarp.
Thereafter, one should worship the mandala of Fire within the pericarp (karṇikā).
One should worship it in sequence with names beginning with the syllables that are the components of the Praṇava.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśvara are to be visualized respectively in the three mandalas.
One should worship oneself as the Inner Self (antarātman) higher and higher.
One should meditate on the Pīṭha-śaktis in the filaments [of the lotus], starting from the east in the middle, in due order;
they hold nooses and goads in their hands and resemble fresh saffron in color.
The Śaktis, beginning with Tīvrā, adorned with jewel ornaments, are to be worshipped: Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, Kāmavardhinī,
Ugratejovatī, Satyā, and the ninth, Vighnanāśinī.
Having uttered the word *sarvaśakti*, one should then pronounce the word *kamalā*.
Having worshipped with "obeisance to Sanāya" using auspicious perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*),
the practitioner of mantra should place the three prior [syllables] in the middle of that completion-seat (*samāptipīṭha*).
Then, by means of the yoga of inhalation (pūraka), having joined the mind to the root [cakra],
one should raise the living consciousness residing there up to the lotus of the heart;
and according to the previously mentioned method, one should [visualize] the illustrious Gaṇeśvara at will.
Having propitiated the gracious Puruṣa with all ritual services,
and having reduced him to the form of his own splendor, he— whose senses are restrained—
elevates the section of mantras and [places it] there within that white lotus.

Having meditated well upon the fire-principle (tejas-tattva) with an unwavering mind, the mantra-practitioner brings it to the position of the bow; then, with his lotus-like hands filled with flowers,
he draws it forth through the flowing channel (pravaha-nāḍī) and places it upon the worshipped lotus-seat.
In the center, one should [visualize] the form with the Gāyatrī mantra; within that, the body of knowledge (vidyādeha);
and within that, the form of supreme consciousness (paracaitanya) by means of the seed-syllable (bīja) in the lotus of the heart.
Having uttered "Mahāgāṇapati," the meaning is "salutation to the Form" (mūrtaye namaḥ).

The wise and excellent practitioner, knowing the mantras, should properly invoke Gaṇeśa from the root as the embodiment of knowledge, and likewise invoke the supreme consciousness according to the path taught by the venerable Guru.
One should place the phonemes of the *tattvas* upon the form, and thereafter, upon the body of the Vidyā.
Having performed the entire ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as before, one should meditate and worship.
Having brought consciousness (*caitanya*) into that [image], one should display the five mudrās.
It is as follows:
Placement, proximity, restraint, and veiling;
thereafter, the transformation into nectar—these are proclaimed as the mudrās.
Then, omniscience is in the heart, and thereafter, satisfaction in Śiva.
The *śikhā* is beginningless awakening, and the weapon arises from infinite power.

Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the heart and other limbs with these *aṅgas* conjoined with their respective seed-syllables according to the rules of instruction, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the root mantra.
Having displayed the Gaṇeśa mudrās and meditated upon the perfect Lord of Ganas, the practitioner of mantra,
while offering a handful of flowers, should again announce his welcome and properly perform the ritual services beginning with water for the feet (pādya).
A seat, a welcome, the arghya offering, water for the feet, water for sipping, honey-mixture, further water for sipping, bathing, garments, ornaments,
as well as fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and prostration.
One should perform the sixteen services (upacāras) for Gaṇeśa.
The ten services, beginning with the water for the feet (pādya) and ending with the food offering (naivedya), are performed in sequence.
The worship consisting of five services consists of those beginning with fragrance (gandha) and ending with the food offering.

Worship is said to be threefold; one should perform at least one of these. Fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice grains, barley, kuśa grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and dūrvā grass—these are declared to be the eight substances for the arghya offering in their proper order.
The water for the feet (pādya) is said to consist of śyāmāka grain, dūrvā grass, lotus, and viṣṇukrāntā;
the water for sipping (ācamanīya) is combined with jasmine, cloves, and kakkola;
and the honey-mixture (madhuparka) is declared to be ghee and curd mixed with honey.
The water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) should be prepared with pure water.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron,
kapirocanā, jaṭāmāṃsī, cora, and cora— these are known as the eight fragrances (gandhāṣṭaka).
Scent is said here to consist of the pastes of sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor;
as well as the flowers of the *karavīra*, the two types of *utpala*, *vijayā*, *punnāga*, *nāga*, *campaka*, *kunda*, and *mandāraka*.
With bandhujīva, javā, uśīra, amānimbha, and kuraṇṭaka; with pāṭala, aśoka, madana, jātikuñja, aparājita,
nandyāvarta, and others— whatever other [flowers] there may be today.
The flowers prescribed in the scriptures are dear to Gaṇeśa;

yet they must not be buds that are withered on all sides, nor those that are decayed, nor those that are defiled. Nor should they be those that have been smelled, touched by the body, or even those that are stale.
The practitioner of mantras should incense [the deity] from below with guggulu, aguru, uśīra, white sugar, clarified butter, honey, and sandalwood, which have been cast onto the embers of heartwood;
and with a wick made of cow’s ghee and sesame oil, containing camphor in its core.
One should display a high, bright lamp that is radiant, fragrant, and pure; one should offer black fragrant incense along with ghee,
white rice, plantains, honey, clarified butter, milk, and so forth.
Then, having made a formal request to the Deity, one should utter "Salutation" (namaḥ) for the bath.
[One should likewise offer] the dressing of the hair, anointing oil, fragrant powder for rubbing, and warm water.
And for the feet, one should say: "O Mahāgaṇapati! Salutation for the water for the feet (pādya)."
In the same manner, one should offer water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with the mantra *svadhā* three times into the mouth;
the respectful offering (*arghya*) with *svāhā* upon the head; the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) likewise with *svadhā*;
and again water for sipping and flowers upon the crown of the head with the *pariśikha* mantra.
Likewise, the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as the sixth, followed by fragrant unguents,
the scent of fragrant myrobalan (āmalakī), water from sacred fords (tīrthodaka),
and divine fragrant ointments— all consecrated with the root mantra.
One should perform an ablution with fragrant red waters from sacred fords (tīrtha),
as well as the beholding of a mirror and other auspicious rites. Thereafter, one should provide divine garments and crowns.
Having awakened [the deity] and assumed the facial expression, the mantra-practitioner should utter, "I perform [this rite].
Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) as before, he should perform the triad beginning with water for the feet (pādya).
With his respective mudrās, he should offer scents, unbroken grains (akṣata), flowers, and incense.
One should worship in sequence with the mantras beginning with the heart and ending with the armor;
having performed the dissolution (*laya*) and the worship according to the number of syllables in the mantra,
and having recited [the mantra] up to the end of the worship of the attendants (*āvaraṇapūjā*), one should then address the deity.
Having worshipped the limbs, the officiant should then worship the outer enclosure;
thereafter, the world-protectors (lokapālas) are to be honored with all the square diagrams.
[They are placed] between Indra and Īśa, as well as between Rākṣasa and Varuṇa.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others are always present upon the bed at the mouth of Brahmā; likewise, the lords of the worlds, beginning with Purandara, along with their respective classes and attendants, should be employed by the wise.

The mantras beginning with the Guru and ending with the World-Protectors (Lokapālas) all commence with the syllable *dhruva* (Oṃ), are joined with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*), and conclude with the dative case and the word *namaḥ*.
Having thus worshipped the enclosure with jasmine flowers, [one should proceed].

Again, one should worship the Deity with the root mantra (mūla-mantra) using perfumes and other offerings correctly. Then, having uttered the mantra "O Mother of Mantras! Victory! Svāhā!", and ringing the bell with the great sounds of the fivefold musical instruments, one should perform the worship.
Having consecrated all the food with the mantra *vanaspati* ending in *svāhā* with its own mudrā,
and with the mantra *suprakāśa* ending in *namaḥ* with its own mudrā,
he [should offer it] to Gaṇeśa in the proper sequence.
Having said, "Accept this food offering at the end, svāhā," the mantra-practitioner should offer everything with his own mudrā and by the ritual bestowal of water; then,
he should visualize the deity together with his retinue as being completely satiated.

Likewise: Now, performing the daily rite, one should carry out the preliminary service (puraścaryā). Having been initiated by the Guru, the practitioner of mantra, well-disciplined as before, should proceed.
A wise person should recite this mantra four hundred and forty-four thousand times for the sake of accomplishing the *puraścaraṇa* rite,
while keeping the head, neck, lips, tongue, eyes, and breath restrained and motionless.
Licking his nose, palate, throat, tongue, lips, and ears;
with his neck slightly raised and his eyes slightly narrowed;
fixing his gaze upon the tip of his nose, he should not let his teeth touch one another.
With his mind fixed on that, his life-breath directed toward that, established in that, and devoted to that, the wise one—
whether by means of speech, in a whisper, or mentally—
should [recite] four thousand [verses], including the forty-fourth.
Or, one who has conquered his senses and subsists on a diet of milk may perform one thousand and eight [recitations];
he should bring that specific measure with which the rite was commenced to its completion.
If he should make it less or more, that man becomes fallen from his vow.
Therefore, one should recite [the mantra] equally until the number is completed;
the lord of practitioners should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) as a tenth part according to the instruction.
When the recitation is thus complete, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as a tenth part.

Together with the previously mentioned rites such as libations (tarpaṇa) and so forth, being devoted to faith, one should feed the Brahmins— along with their attendants (sāṅga)— according to the number appropriate for the ritual, following the sequence to be described, with joyful minds.

One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru according to one's means. Having obtained the guru’s compassion, that best among those who know mantras should thereafter recite [the mantra] four times, or else daily according to his own capacity.

The mantra-practitioner, constantly worshipping Vighneśvara with great diligence through offerings such as worship and fire-oblations (homa) according to the rules, without stinginess regarding wealth,
shall enjoy great prosperity free from obstacles within a year.
If the performance of the fire-ritual (agnikārya) was previously completed by Bali according to the injunctions, then,

having offered oblations with the concluding mantras into the fire consecrated by the rite, one should today satisfy [the deity] three times according to the previous sequence while seated upon the mantra-throne.
"By those who are fit" means by those devoted to the performance of the respective mantras.
The ritual applications (*prayoga*) are also found in that very same [text]:
"In this manner, the practitioner whose mantra is perfected should accomplish the rites for desired ends."
I shall indeed describe the rites for the fulfillment of desires for the benefit of practitioners,
according to the path prescribed in the scriptures, in brief and not at length.
Within the lotus of one's own heart, [one should meditate upon] Gaṇeśāna, whose radiance is as white as a jasmine flower or the moon.
For one who meditates without interruption upon [the deity] adorned with white ornaments,
the Goddess of Speech— beautiful in her extraction of the flood of scriptures and bestowing divine knowledge— truly shines forth eternally within his lotus-like mouth.
The most excellent of mantra-practitioners should not exclude Gaṇeśāna, who possesses a luster like vermilion; having meditated upon him as holding a noose and a goad,
the woman of exquisite form approaches him, endowed with the essence of passion.

He who meditates upon Him—who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; who resembles snow, the kunda flower, and the moon; who is irreproachable and possesses a noble luster; and who is adorned with shimmering rubies—under his control fall even the most excellent women.

In disputes, while meditating upon Gaṇeśāna, who possesses a radiance equal to blazing fire, within the mouth of the opponent, one should mentally recite the mantra. He will quickly paralyze that person's speech; even if the disputant is weak, it shall not be otherwise.
Having meditated upon Gaṇeśāna, who is the size of a thumb, resembles pure crystal, and is the nectar-essence of the sky of consciousness,
one should constantly bathe that best of gods upon the surface of the earth.
Freed from all diseases, he lives for a long time.
[One should meditate on] Gaṇeśāna, white in color, with ten arms, fierce with pride,
wearing white garments, gentle, and drenched in the nectar of the lunar consciousness.
With a pure mind, the practitioner should constantly meditate upon [the deity] in the lotus of the heart;
like Garuḍa, he instantly destroys the three kinds of poison.
One seeking gold should always offer honey, while one seeking subjugation should offer milk-rice oblations.

With ghee, one should offer oblations for the attainment of Lakṣmī; likewise with sugar for longevity and the accomplishment of wealth. A wise person should offer with curd for the sake of prosperity, and with food for the attainment of food. For the acquisition of wealth, one should offer sesame seeds and rice.

One desiring rain should offer oblations with salt during a drought; one desiring prosperity should likewise offer parched grain, safflower, and mustard seeds. One seeking power over others should sacrifice with lotuses, and thus bring even a king under one's control.
His wife was exhilarated by the vast, manifest, and auspicious white water-lilies.
From the oblation of fuel-sticks produced from the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *nyagrodha* trees,
the brahmins, kṣatriyas, vaiśyas, and śūdras indeed become instantly submissive.

Having fashioned an image of women out of flour every day, by means of an oblation of clarified butter, women come under his control; it is not otherwise. Having recited the King of Mantras, the dissolution [of the rite] is performed according to the charming procedure.
The mantra-practitioner should offer oblations ten times the number [of recitations] with mustard seeds and salt;
then, taking that ash with his left hand, he should strike the woman.
That woman, her eyes languid with passion, will come to him.
Likewise, the knower of mantras should offer this with yellow flowers;
he shall paralyze the enemy army along with its ministers, forces, and mounts,
and by the power of this mantra, the opponent shall become mute.
One should paralyze the five divine [elements]; there is no need for deliberation here.
A wise person, using fuel-sticks of *vibhītaka*, should perform oblations with discipline;
he will certainly and completely expel enemies from their own places, of this there is no doubt.
Equal to Mount Meru and Mandara, this [mantra] uproots [the enemy] and not otherwise.
Whether in a village, in battle, or even in a city, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) after praising this;
it uproots with speed, so what need is there to mention [its power] over mere mortals?
Having carefully inscribed the name of the enemy upon a nimba leaf with the blood of a cow,
a horse, or a buffalo, combined with nimba oil,
one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) in a secluded place twenty thousand times.
He who possesses such a staff becomes like Manmatha himself and is hated by the worlds.
One should take a peg made of human bone, properly measured at eight finger-breadths,
wrap it with the hair of a corpse, and empower it one thousand and eight times with mantras.
At the time of the arising of the Kulika, one should dig into the earth at the gate of the enemy;
his death will occur within seven days—contemplate this, for there is no doubt here.
Now, I shall briefly describe the method for the entry of the maiden.
In a well-concealed and solitary place, one should smear the ground with cow dung.
The preceptor, having become purified, well-bathed, and having subdued his senses,
should take a new jar and fill it with a pure jar [of water].
Having brought a new earthen bowl filled with the milk of a tawny cow (kapilā),
and having placed it upon a water-pot, one should then light a lamp;
this should be done by youths or young girls while reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Whatever has occurred in the past, will occur in the future, and exists in the present—all auspicious and inauspicious things—they behold; of this there is no doubt.
Having meditated correctly upon Gaṇeśāna, one should recite [the mantra] during the final watch of the night.

Auspicious and inauspicious karmas are declared by these [omens], there is no doubt. One desiring a daughter, having become pure, should recite the king of mantras of Gaṇeśa ten thousand times with [the flowers] born from the red-horse-plant (raktāśvamāra) gathered in a net.
By performing a fire sacrifice with flowers ten times [the prescribed number], one certainly obtains that maiden.
I shall now describe the method for procuring elephants for kings:
a king should have an elephant-ocean constructed within his forest.
Having meditated upon a vast pit, the Guru should then,
in a beautiful pavilion endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics,
have an auspicious quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) constructed to the north of the altar.
Having invoked Gaṇeśa upon the upper part of the altar, the knower of mantras should offer well-cooked fruits, water, and prepared food. Then,
having established the fire there as before, the practitioner of mantras [should proceed].
With forty thousand oblations consisting of eight substances anointed with the three sweets,
and with four thousand, four hundred and forty-four oblations of each individual substance respectively, one should perform the fire-offering for five days.
One who knows the tantras and mantras should cause the best of the twice-born to perform the recitation;
by the grace of Gaṇeśvara, within forty days,
those who are terrified of the *kalas* fall like golden [objects] upon the great banyan tree.
One should constantly feed Brāhmaṇas with deliciously prepared foods;
by the blessings bestowed by those Brāhmaṇas, that lord of the earth prospers.
And one should give fifty cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to their preceptor.

The preceptor, having bathed and worshipped the deity with clarified butter using the mantras beginning with *mithuna* and ending with the lords of the directions (*digīśa*), should properly complete the fire-offering (*homa*)— using either a tenth part of that measurement or the wealth obtained from its sale.
Having offered [the oblation] again when only a muhūrta remains, he should perform the rites as before.
Having again offered a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali) into the lotus of his own heart,
the mantra-practitioner should dismiss Gaṇeśvara, and the Guru should dismiss the fire.
Having offered all the implements for the fire sacrifice to the preceptor with a pure mind,
and having prostrated again and again,
the king [honored him] with other auspicious gifts such as ornaments, silk garments, and the like.
One should properly satisfy the preceptor for the great increase of elephants;
thus he prospers together with the classes of kṣatriyas and the kingdom.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sādhana of Mahālakṣmī and the others.
In a pleasing, solitary place, free from all disturbances, [the practitioner],
wearing white garments and adorned with white garlands and unguents, [should proceed].
Having performed his daily rites, the practitioner, having established the fire as before,
[should offer] five lotuses smeared with the three sweets, and five times five *śrīphala* fruits bound together with a focused mind, combined with honey, clarified butter, and milk.
On the first day of the bright fortnight, one should offer oblations in the morning with a one-pointed mind.
One attains inexhaustible and great prosperity; of this there is no doubt.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Mothers beginning from the first day as prescribed, and having performed the great worship of Śrī Gaṇeśa on the fourth day.
With the aforementioned substances smeared with the three sweets, starting from the first day of the bright fortnight— that is,
from the *pratipad*—
one should continue until one hundred and eight lakhs have been completed in whatever time it takes.

For that duration, the practitioner, with a serene mind, should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) in this manner. At the conclusion of the *homa*, he will certainly behold his own Lakṣmī and his treasure.
Standing facing the sun, with arms raised and facing the east, he should remain thus.
By reciting this mantra one hundred thousand times, the practitioner shall obtain great wealth.
On his own birthday, or every day at dawn, the person should offer oblations of milk, clarified butter, and dūrvā grass.
Free from disease and having conquered death, he lives a long life upon this earth;
one whose self is purified during the time sacred to Brahmā, on the full moon day of a festival,
[should take] pure cow-dung of Kapila [color] onto a lotus leaf placed upon the ground.
Having taken [the substance] over which the mantra has been recited ten thousand times, one should bury it in the ground.
There, no fear exists from spirits, thieves, serpents, or the like. First, the wise man should daily offer oblations to Mahāgaṇeśāna,
having extracted the Vetālas, Siddhas, and Kulikas from the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
The preeminent practitioner always obtains highly fortunate things on earth;

likewise, the ointment of accomplishment (*siddhāñjana*), the sword, the sandals, and so forth— which are difficult to obtain anywhere in the three worlds— belong to this lord of practitioners at all times.
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the King of Yantras belonging to the Lord of Gaṇas.
On a perfectly level, pure ground, well-adorned with perfumes and other offerings,
one who is free from desire and anger should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as previously described.

Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, the Lord of the gods of gods and son of Śaṅkara, one should extract the King of Mantras upon birch bark with auspicious materials. [The substances are: musk, gorocanā, camphor, saffron, sandalwood, and liquid.
With all these ingredients— mixed with the essence of cow dung and blended with elephant ichor—
and having made them perfectly uniform, one should fill the vessel with breath and draw [the design] using a pen,
a golden needle, a *jātī* wood stick, or *dūrvā* grass.
One should draw a thirty-six-pointed figure, then an eight-spoked one, and after that a twelve-spoked one;
furthermore, one should write the letters of the *gāyatrī* beginning with the *ka*-group on the outside.
One should then fashion a great earth-maṇḍala adorned with eight elephants.

Outside of that, the practitioner of mantra should draw the auspicious Varuṇa-kūrma-maṇḍala. Within the pericarp (karṇikā), he should write the syllables *ha* and *kṣa*, encircled by the *praṇava* (oṃ).
He should place the six limbs (*aṅga*) in the six corners and write the Lakṣmī-mantra upon the petals.
One should write the power (śakti) on the twelve-spoked [wheel], excluding the neuter vowels;
then, on the petals of the [twelve] digits, one should write the series of vowels. Thereafter, on the eight-petalled lotus, one should write all the letters from *ka* to *ma*, starting from the east.
Furthermore, one should draw the same [diagram] on the sides and corners.
This yantra has been fully described; it must not be given to just anyone.
It was previously taught by Śiva for the pacification of all obstacles.
Having encased it with the three metals and performed the rite of infusing life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*),
the man who wears this yantra— over which the *amṛta* mantra has been recited—
all his obstacles, diseases, and calamities shall perish.
Kings fall under one's control, and the wives of others are agitated;
even lions and other predatory beasts, thieves, venomous snakes, and intoxicated elephants,
as well as all castes beginning with the twice-born— even powerful enemies— [are subdued].
By the mere sight of him, they always come under his control;
then there proceeds speech in Sanskrit, Prākṛta, and other languages,
crowded with parasols, chowries, crowns, garlands, staffs, and so forth.
Mahālakṣmī herself serves him with power for a long time;
it is impossible to describe the power of this collection of yantras,
for there is nothing on this earth that cannot be accomplished by means of this mantra.
I shall now describe the method of attraction; let it be applied by means of this yantra.
Having first drawn the yantra with beautiful red substances mixed with the blood of the ring finger, one should inscribe the name of the person to be acted upon.
Having worshipped with red flowers mixed with red sandalwood,
and having placed the yantra within the belly of an image made of beeswax,
the best of mantra-knowers should duly install the Wind-god (Samīraṇa).
One should heat the four corners with a lamp of *kapilā* cow's ghee for three days, until it no longer melts.
On the seventh day, even if she were Tilottamā herself, the woman would appear before one.
Having recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should heat it and then wear it;
she will remain under his control like a servant until the end of his life.
With a concentrated mind, one should inscribe the yantra on a stone slab using yellow pigments.
Having placed [the substance] upon *arka* leaves and worshipped it with yellow flowers,
and having wrapped it in a yellow cloth, one may paralyze even weapons;
one may likewise paralyze *dānavas*, *grahas*, thieves, and even an army.
Having brought together the life-force and blood of those who are at enmity without cause, one becomes a calculator; the seer is Ṛṣi, the meter is Nivṛt, and its deity is Vighna.
The letter *ga* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the bindu is the power (*śakti*).
The Gaṇeśa Gāyatrī:
We know the one with a single tusk; we meditate upon the one with the elephant's trunk; may that Vighna inspire us.

Having mixed charcoal from a cremation ground with that [substance], one should write the name of the target together with the ritual action using a crow’s wing-feather within the cavity of a funeral pyre. When this yantra is cast at a solitary linga or a banner, it will certainly cause the target to be driven away.
It also brings about enmity from the world; of this there is no doubt.
The knower of rites [should draw] the yantra on a cloth from a cremation ground with a pin made of human bone, or with charcoal from a funeral pyre produced from a poisonous tree.
Having become angry and having drawn [the figure], one should bury it in the ground in a cremation ground;
within seven days the enemy dies—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having extracted this [image] and washed it with milk, the practitioner of the vow should consume it.
I shall now describe another meditation on the Lord of the Gaṇas, which accomplishes all aims:
[one should meditate on] the God who resembles a fresh cloud, possessing a luster like crushed collyrium,
having eighteen arms, and being like Mount Meru or Mandara.
With a terrifying face and deformed eyes, possessing a voice like the roar of clouds,
he was clothed in red garments and wore a sacred thread of serpents;
he blazed with various jewels and was radiant with a crown ornament.
He holds a spear and an axe with his power, as well as a javelin and a threatening gesture;
he bears a noose and a goad resting upon his tusk-lotuses, along with a bow of sugarcane,
his own flower-arrows, the tip of a stalk of rice, and a vessel filled with sweetmeats.

The elephant-faced Lord of Gods, seated upon a lotus throne and saluted by all the deities, holds a water-pot with his own trunk, as well as a water-jar, a rosary, and displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons with his auspicious hands.
The mantra-practitioner should contemplate in this manner for the pacification of all calamities;
[one should visualize] red for the rites of subjugation and attraction, yellow for the rite of immobilization,
smoke-colored for hatred and expulsion, and black for the killing of an enemy.
One should know that a golden-hued [image] bestows wealth, while a white one grants knowledge;
thus should the wise person contemplate for the successful completion of each respective rite.
In the thirteenth chapter of the Śāradātilaka.
They know the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati to be "pañcāntaka" joined with "śaśidhara.
"Pañcāntaka" is the letter *ga*;
"śaśin" is the nasal drop (*bindu*), and it is conjoined with that.
Alternatively, "Śaśī" (the moon) is the visarga;
for it is said that "Śakti" is the moon.
This extraction is thus provided for the sake of concealment.
Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that these two— the ritual application of worship and so forth— spoken by Uttaragārgya, are common to both [traditions].
Some, however, say they are joined with the vowel *au*.
And it is said in the *Prayogasāra*:
"The seed-syllable joined with the moon (the vowel *a*) and likewise with the third consonant (*ka*).
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by means of the seed-syllables endowed with the six long vowels.
Having the luster of vermilion, three eyes, and a broad belly; holding a tusk, a noose, a goad, and the gesture of granting boons with his lotus-like hands;

beautiful with a citron fruit shimmering in his great hand; with a crescent moon illuminating his crest; having the face of a lordly elephant; and with cheeks moistened by a citron fruit—[I bow to Gaṇeśa].
Worship Gaṇapati, whose ornaments are bound with the lord of serpents, and who is clad in red garments and red unguents.
Rāghavabhaṭṭa, however, describes the mudrā to be shown after meditation as follows:
"Having placed the hand hanging down from the mouth with the fingers contracted,
the thumb should be positioned between the middle finger and the index finger, or else below the middle finger."
This mudrā of Gaṇeśa, which bestows all accomplishments (siddhis), is now described;
alternatively,
it is a fist from which the thumb has emerged at the joint of the index and middle fingers.
"With the face turned downward and the form elongated, the middle finger is the mudrā of obstacles.
Or alternatively:
"By joining the root of the hand, whose tip is curled, with the nose..."
"The Gaṇeśvarī mudrā shall be the bestower of all accomplishments.
Thus it is said;
this [mudrā] is common to the mantras of all Gaṇapatis.
In the Śāradā [Tantra].
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and then perform a fire sacrifice with a tenth part of that amount,
using sweetmeats (modaka), flattened rice (pṛthuka), parched grain (lāja), groats (saktu),
sugarcane joints, coconuts, pure sesame seeds, and ripe plantains.
The wise have declared that there are eight substances of an obstacle.
Regarding this, Rāghavabhaṭṭa maintains that the oblation should be offered with each substance individually, combined with half-mardana;
however, some say that the oblation should be performed by combining all eight substances.

Because this would lead to the contingency of doubt regarding the measure of each respective oblation, and because there are two distinct actions for each at the root, it is impossible to perform the eight-dravya homa as a single composite entity, since that would constitute a different substance altogether.
This has been stated by Bhadrācārya:
"The sacrifice would not be performed with rice alone, nor with the materials exactly as they are heard [in the texts];
for if it were to be performed with mixed materials, there is no scriptural injunction for such mixing."
If it is argued that, in the case of the *trimadhura* oblation, even that which is mixed with the three sweets (*trimadhu*) should not be performed, we say: not so.
For there is the scriptural injunction: "Every substance for the oblation is declared to be accompanied by the three sweets.

As for the mixing [of the substances], it is like the lack of connection between the portions (*avadāna*) of the animal sacrifice and the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), due to their being separated by other intervening rites.
Because there is no contradiction with the procedure for the *jyāmelana* (the union of the bowstrings).
As it has been stated in the *Gaṇeśavimarṣiṇī*:
"One should offer oblations separately and separately with the eight substances smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). (p. 609)
By the word "pure" (*śuddhaiḥ*), it is stated that one should remove dust and wash [the materials] until they are purified. In the *Śāradā-tantra*:
"And on a sacred seat (*pīṭha*) endowed with the intense and other powers, one should worship Vighneśvara."
Tīvrā, Jvālinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, Kāmarūpiṇī,
Ugrā, Tejovatī, Satyā, and the ninth, Vighnanāśinī.
Their meditation is described by Rāghavabhaṭṭa:
"The Śaktis beginning with Tīvrā, resembling fresh saffron in hue, adorned with jewel ornaments, and holding a noose, a goad, and joined palms in their hands, should be worshipped."
In the Śāradā [Tantra]: "From 'sarvādi' up to 'śaktikamalāsanāya' ending with the heart [syllable], this is the seat-mantra (pīṭhamantra);
by means of this, one should offer a seat to the Lord."
Having conceptualized the form by means of the root mantra, one should worship Vighneśa within it;
first, one should worship these [deities] in the four directions upon the pericarp,
and thereafter, one should worship the deities of the limbs (aṅgadevatās) in due order upon the filaments.
One should worship Vakratuṇḍa and the others within the center of the vessel according to the prescribed rule.
Regarding the phrase "according to the prescribed rule," Rāghavabhaṭṭa states that it means "with the seed-syllable of Gaṇapati.
[The deities are] Vakratuṇḍa, Ekadaṃṣṭra, Mahādeva, and Gajānana.
Immediately thereafter, one should worship the formidable Vighnarāja known as Lambodara,
who is smoke-colored, at the tips of the petals; then one should worship Brāhmī and the other goddesses,
followed by the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons— thus one should worship the deity.
One who has mastered the mantra should perform the ritual applications enjoined by the *kalpa*.
An oblation (*homa*) performed with coconuts on the fourth lunar day shall bestow prosperity.
Beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight, the pure and wise practitioner [should proceed].
One should offer four hundred oblations, ending with the dative case, using coconut, sugar-candy, parched rice, and sesame seeds respectively; all living beings will become submissive.
However, there is a specific distinction regarding rites for subjugation (*vaśya*) and the like.
In the *Prayogasāra* and the *Nārāyaṇīya*, it is stated:

"Having duly brought the object of accomplishment here with the noose and the goad, one who desires subjugation should stand above him and recite [the mantra]; this procedure instantly destroys the anger of one who is enraged."
An oblation of sesame seeds and rice grains bestows the power to bring Lakṣmī under one's control.
Here too, the oblation consists of four hundred offerings, beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight and ending on the fourth.
An oblation of parched grain mixed with the three sweets (trimadhura) procures a maiden [as a wife].
In this context, there is a fire-oblation (*homa*) of four hundred [offerings] beginning from the first day up to the seventh;
likewise, as cited by Rāghavabhaṭṭa: "for seven days with parched grains (*lāja*) sprinkled with the three sweets (*madhuratraya*)."
By this procedure, one obtains the desired bride or groom;

a homa performed with oblations smeared with clarified butter shall accomplish the desires of men. For four days, one should perform a homa with offerings stirred and tossed in curd, according to the rule of the sages.
Beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad) up to the fourth,
one who performs this with the root of the white Arka tree and red sandalwood wood will likewise always bring about great affection and ensure complete subjugation.
Having fashioned [an image] from Nimba wood broken by an elephant or from ivory,

and having worshipped Vighneśvara, the practitioner of mantra, while fasting, should recite [the mantra] during a lunar eclipse; then, touching it and wearing it upon his crest-lock, he should proceed.
In battles, legal proceedings, and so forth, one shall obtain victory and prosperity.
As for the recitation (*japa*), it continues from the first morsel of food until liberation. Likewise:
Having recited this mantra over it, [one should apply] the bezoar mixed with honey.
Intoxication is elephant-ichor.
By the rite of applying the *tilaka*, one brings all men under one's control.
One should write the name within the seed-syllables arranged in both direct and reverse order;
having worshipped it in fresh butter (*navanīta*), one should touch it and recite the *prāṇamantra*.
Having further recited the root mantra one hundred and eight times,
one should consume that iron while observing the practice for seven days during the night;
he will quickly become submissive to the practitioner, there is no doubt.

By the word "anuloma" (in direct order), it is merely stated that the two seed-syllables are enclosed; the intended meaning is that one should write the name of the person to be accomplished between the two seed-syllables, like butter.
In the first Brāhmaṇa chapter of the Gāyatrī Tantra.
The twice-born should worship Gaṇeśa with the sixteen types of offerings;
he should worship the Son of Śiva with the great mantras beginning with *aṇimā*.
Having meditated upon Him and offered water for the feet and other requisites, he should recite the mantra beginning with *aṇimā*.
Resembling the color of vermilion, endowed with a yogic cloth,
pot-bellied, of massive body, with a face like the trunk of an elephant,
possessed of the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and others, having eight arms and three eyes.
One who desires liberation should worship the Liṅga consecrated by Vijayā.
Oṃ aṃ gaṇapataye svāhā. With this very mantra, one should worship Gaṇanāyaka;
and with the eight mantras beginning with aṇimā, one should fully worship the eight-armed deity.
Oṃ, obeisance to Aṇimā, Svāhā! Praṃ, obeisance to Prāpti, Svāhā! Maṃ, obeisance to Mahimā, Svāhā!
Īṃ, obeisance to the power of lordship, svāhā! Vaṃ, obeisance to the power of control, svāhā! Kaṃ, obeisance to the power of fulfilling desires, svāhā!
Having thus worshipped according to the rule, the practitioner should employ the desired mantras, having fed [the deities] according to the ritual with various desirable fruits and the like,
with delicious cakes made of fine rice flour, and with curd, milk, ghee, and so forth.
He worshipped the mouse with flowers of divine fragrance, with ointments of divine scent,
and with various desirable fruits and other offerings.
Oṃ maṃ, to the rat, the vehicle of Gaṇādhipa, the King of Dharma, svāhā!
With this very mantra, one should always worship the rat.
Now follows Haridrāgaṇeśa.
Regarding their origin, in the tenth chapter of the *Nāradapañcarātra*, Nārada said:
"The origin of the script of Lambodara has now been told to me;
tell me the origin of the other forms of the Lords of the Gaṇas."
Brahmā said:
Once, the goddess Pārvatī, having ground a superior turmeric,
fashioned a doll from that yellow pigment;
then that virtuous lady said to Śaṅkara, "O Śaṅkara, protect your son!"
Thus addressed by his beloved, Śambhu caused that son to grow;
and with supreme affection, he spoke regarding the purification of the body:
"O fortunate one, perform penance! Thereby you shall attain perfection."
Brahmā said:
Having heard his father’s words, he sat down auspiciously and departed quickly from there to perform austerities at Kāmākhyā on the mountain of Kāmarūpa;
being self-controlled and pure, he worshipped the five-syllabled Ugratārā.
Then, having quickly attained direct perception [of him],
Śiva, the Lord of Girijā, spoke with affection to that son:
"Without doubt, you are the bestower of the four aims of life to practitioners."
Just as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Supreme Goddess,
as well as all other deities, bestow the fruits of the four aims of life,
so too are you, O Lord of Gods, the bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life.
He is renowned in all the Agamas and other scriptures as Haridrāgaṇanātha; likewise, the god is known as Lipilambodara and Heramba.
Furthermore, that form of these deities which is known as their state of childhood is designated as Ucchiṣṭagaṇanātha within the scope of the scriptures.
Now begins the Mahāgaṇapati Upaniṣad. Om Laṃ Svāhā! May [Gaṇeśa] protect us both, Svāhā! May He nourish us both, Svāhā! May we acquire spiritual power together, Svāhā!
May our study be full of splendor; may we not hate one another.
Om, peace, peace, peace.
Om Laṃ, salutations to Gaṇapati; you alone are the manifest, you are he.
You alone are the sole creator; you alone are the sole sustainer; you alone are the sole destroyer.
You indeed are all this; you are Brahman.

You are the manifest Self, eternally; I speak the *ṛta*, I speak the truth. Protect me; protect the speaker; protect the listener; protect the giver. [Protect me] as one who is not foolish, though talkative.
Protect the disciple from behind, protect from the front, and protect from above.
From the south,
from above, from below, and from beneath that which is below—
protect me from every side, protect me on all sides!
You are composed of speech, you are composed of consciousness, you are Brahman;
you are composed of Brahman, you are composed of bliss, you are the non-dual existence-consciousness-bliss.
You are the perceptible Brahman; you are composed of knowledge and composed of realized wisdom.
This entire world is born from you;
