this entire world will dissolve into you.
You are earth, fire, air, and space.
You are the four [organs]: speech, hands, anus, and feet;
you are beyond the three qualities (guṇas);
you are beyond the three bodies (dehas).
You transcend the three periods of time;
you abide eternally in the *mūlādhāra*; you consist of the nature of the three powers (*śakti*); the yogis meditate upon you eternally.
You are Brahmā, you are Viṣṇu, you are Rudra, you are Indra, you are Agni, you are Vāyu, you are Sūrya, you are Candramas; you are Brahman, Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ, Om.
Having first uttered the *gaṇas* and so forth, and immediately thereafter the *varṇas* and so forth,
followed by the *anusvāra*, one should likewise contemplate that which is adorned with the crescent moon;
this is your form as Manu.
The letter *ga* is the initial form;
the letter *a* is the middle form;
and the *anusvāra* is the final form.
The bindu is the form that transcends [the phonemes];
the nāda is the joining;
the saṃhitā is the conjunction.
This is the Vidyā of Īśāna-Gaṇeśa.
Gaṇaka is the Ṛṣi; Niyūḍgāyatrī is the Chandas. *Gaṃ*, obeisance to Gaṇapati.
We know the One-Tusked One; we meditate upon the Crooked-Trunked One.
May that Danti inspire us.
He has one tusk and four hands, bearing a noose and a goad;
with his hands he displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons, and he has a rat as his banner.
Red in color, with a protruding belly and ears like winnowing baskets, clad in red garments,
his limbs smeared with red perfumes and well-worshipped with red flowers—
the God who is compassionate toward devotees, the creator of the universe, the infallible Acyuta.
He who constantly meditates thus upon that which was manifested at the beginning of creation— transcending both Prakṛti and Puruṣa— is a yogi, the best among yogis.
Oṃ, homage to the Lord of Boars; homage to Gaṇapati; homage to the First Lord;
let there be salutation to you, the pot-bellied one.
Homage to the one with a single tusk, the destroyer of obstacles, the son of Śiva, the embodiment of the bestower of boons.
Furthermore, O Sovereign of All! whoever studies this very [text] becomes fit for the state of Brahman;
he is liberated from the five great sins;
he prospers in happiness in every respect.
Studying in the evening, one destroys the evil committed during the day;
studying in the morning, one destroys the evil committed during the night.
Thus, by studying both in the evening and in the morning, even a sinner becomes sinless.
When recited everywhere, one becomes free from obstacles; one attains dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. This Atharvaśīrṣa is not to be given to one who is not a disciple.
Whoever gives this for the sake of delusion becomes more wicked.
But by reciting it a thousand times, whatever desire one studies, that very thing one attains.
With this, one consecrates Gaṇapati; he becomes composed of speech.

"One who recites [the mantra] while fasting on the fourth lunar day becomes possessed of knowledge"— this is the statement from the *Atharvavaṇa*. Furthermore, one who performs worship with sprouts of *dūrvā* grass, practicing the Brahma-mantras and so forth, thinking "knowledge never fears," becomes like Vaiśravaṇa.
He who sacrifices with parched grain becomes possessed of fame;
he becomes wise.
He who sacrifices with a thousand sweetmeats attains his desire.
He who sacrifices with clarified butter and fuel-sticks obtains everything.
Having properly instructed eight Brahmins, one becomes radiant as the sun.
By reciting [the mantra] during a solar eclipse at a great river or in the presence of an image, he...
The mantra becomes effective;
he is liberated from great evil and becomes all-knowing.
"He who knows this"—thus says the Upanishad—may it protect us both.
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Thus ends the Mahāgaṇapati Upaniṣad.
Now follows the hymn to Gaṇapati.
In the Nāradapañcarātra, in the seventh chapter of the first rātra.
The venerable Nārada said:
O Gaṇeśa! O best of gods! O Lambodara! O one higher than the highest!
O Heramba! O source of auspiciousness! O elephant-faced one! O three-eyed one!
O son of the three-eyed one! O bestower of prosperity! O you who are desired by the remembrance of Śrīdhara!
O Supreme Bliss! O Delighter of the Supreme Pārvatī! You Yourself! Worthy of worship everywhere! Worshiped by all in the world! O Teacher of the World!
O Lord of the World! O Seed of the World! O Protector of the World! Salutations be unto You!
I bow to Him whose worship is foremost of all, who is praised by all yogis,
and who is honored by the lords of the gods and the lords of sages;
solely through the supreme adoration of Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul.
I bow to that best of gods, the most excellent and most venerable one, whom the virtuous Pārvatī attained through meritorious rites and vows;
I bow to that Lord of the Gaṇas, the best among people and the most eminent.
This hymn to Lambodara was composed by Nārada in ancient times.
If one recites it daily at the time of worship, victory attends him at every step.
Indeed, he who, being well-disciplined, recites it for one year with a firm resolve, [attains his desires].
One obtains an excellent son who is supremely devoted to Kṛṣṇa—
one who is illustrious, learned, wealthy, and long-lived.
For such a person, obstacles shall be destroyed, and there shall be great sovereignty and stainless fame.
Having enjoyed its fruit right here, one goes at the end to the abode of Hari.
Thus ends the Gaṇeśa-stotra in the Jñānāmṛtasāra.
Now, the characteristics of the *vāṇaliṅga*,
as recorded in the *Kālottara* cited in the *Vīramitrodaya*.
Likewise, the Bāṇaliṅga should be known as the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Now hear the origin and the characteristics of the Bāṇaliṅga from me at length,
as well as those of [the liṅgas] from the Narmadā, Devikā, Gaṅgā, and Yamunā.
O Six-faced One, there exist Vāṇaliṅgas of the rivers of merit;
they are worshipped here by Indra and the other gods and are marked with their respective signs.
Śiva, the bestower of all goals, is ever present there.
They say those are the marks of Indra, which bestow the fruit of universal sovereignty.
Thus ends the definition of the characteristic marks of Indra.
Auspicious, red, constantly dripping [nectar], and hot, it bestows abundant peace.
Resembling a spear or marked with the emblem of a spear,
by installing this excellent Liṅga, one becomes a sovereign of splendor.
Thus ends the definition of the characteristics of the Āgneya-liṅga. || 2 ||
The southern [direction] may be shaped like a staff or like a tongue;
if that which has been spoken together with them is not purified, then it is known that by being established,
death is brought about through that which has been poured out.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the Yāmya liṅga.
The Rākṣasa liṅga is like a sword and bestows the fruits of knowledge and yoga;
it is coated with gravel and the like, blunt, and likewise possesses a bulging belly.
The sign of a Rākṣasa marriage is for the sake of expiation; it does not bring honor to the state of a householder.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the Nairṛta-liṅga. || 4 ||
The [mandala] of Varuṇa is circular in shape, marked with a noose, and possesses the luster of a row [of flames];
it belongs to one's own [domain] starting from the eastern gate, while its attainment through enjoyment resides in the center.
Thus ends the definition of the characteristics of the Varuṇa-liṅga.
Black, smoky, fresh, and pleasing, resembling a banner—
such a mace-banner was placed upon his head, while others, increasingly inferior, were scattered here and there.
Thus ends the definition of the characteristics of the mark of Vāyu.
It has the form of a cotton-wool club, heavy in the middle, and contains within it the *śaṣa* grain of the god of wealth.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the Kuvera-liṅga. || 7 ||
Whether by day or by night, there is growth and strength for the crops;
yet it is fierce, marked by pain in the bones, and possesses the luster of frost and earrings.
Thus ends the definition of the characteristics of the Raudra-linga. || 8 ||
Alternatively, it is known that the Vaiṣṇava [image] consists of the four castes;
it is adorned with the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, and other [emblems],
marked with the Śrīvatsa and the Kaustubha gem, and inscribed with all the lion-thrones.
Alternatively, that which bears the mark of Vainateya or is likewise marked with the foot of Viṣṇu is called Vaiṣṇava;
it bestows the fruit of all sovereignty.
Thus ends the definition of the Vaiṣṇava liṅga. || 9 ||
The moon situated upon a śālagrāma stone and so forth, which increases prosperity,
brings fortune when marked with a lotus, a svastika, or the śrīvatsa.
Thus also is the definition of the Vaiṣṇava liṅga. || 10 ||
In the section on characteristics (*lakṣaṇakāṇḍa*) contained within the *Hemādri*.
Nārada said:
Now, O Brahmin, I shall describe to you the supreme eleventh sign,
by hearing which all sins go to destruction at that very moment;
it has the hue of honey-pigment and is endowed with black curls.
It is declared to be the self-manifested Liṅga (Svayambhūliṅga), frequented by all the Siddhas. || 1 ||
Adorned with various colors and endowed with matted locks and tridents,
it is the Liṅga named Mṛtyuñjaya, saluted by gods and demons alike.
Long in shape, white in color, and marked with black spots—this is known as Nīlakaṇṭha, a Liṅga worthy of worship by gods and demons alike. || 3 ||
He was white in luster with white hair, endowed with three eyes;
he is the three-eyed Mahādeva, the dispeller of all sins.
A blazing liṅga with matted locks, dark-hued and of massive form—this is declared to be Kālāgnirudra, who is served by all living beings. (5)
He has the luster of a honey-colored tawny hue, wears a white sacred thread,
is seated upon a white lotus, is adorned with a crescent moon,
is equipped with the weapon of universal dissolution, and is known by the name Tripurāri.
Brilliantly white in luster, with tawny matted hair, wearing a garland of skulls, the supreme Lord Īśāna bears a trident; he is the Liṅga who accomplishes all goals.
Holding a trident and a ḍamaru drum, with the left half white and the right half red,
he is known as Ardhanārīśvara, the bestower of desired boons upon all the gods.
Slightly reddish, lovely, thick, long, and brilliantly radiant—
this is declared to be Mahākāla, the bestower of virtue, desire, wealth, and liberation.
This mark of the Linga of the Great Lord has been described to you;
by this alone one becomes fulfilled—what need is there for many, O observer of noble vows?
Thus are the marks of the Bāṇaliṅga.
In the Kālottara as cited in the Vīramitrodaya.

One should employ a vessel marked with the aforementioned signs for the sake of spiritual welfare, but one should avoid a vessel marked with the head of a sage (śīrṣa-mantra). A liṅga marked with the letter *ya*,
or a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) marked with the letter *ya* or the staff (*daṇḍa*), or one bearing the mark of the sacred thread (*sūtra*), is considered to be endowed with the knowledge of Brahman.

Mahākāla is moon-colored; Nandīśa is like a ruby. All [of them] resemble rubies, possess great splendor, and are worshipped by the Siddhas. [Others] have the luster of pearls or the hue of sapphires, and are worshipped by the Rudras and Ādityas.
Adored by the Vasus, Indra, the lords of the Yakṣas, the Guhyakas, and the Yātudhānas,
it is multicolored, blue, and possesses the luster of the lunar orb;
such is the characteristic of the Bāṇaliṅga.
As recorded in the Vīramitrodaya.
This is the characteristic declared by those expert in the principles of examination:
if balance-equilibrium is not achieved after three, seven, or five attempts, then it is called *vāṇa*; otherwise, it is of the nature of stone (*pāṣāṇa*).
The measurement is by means of rice.
Regarding other scales and so forth, if the rice [weighed] on them is greater, then that linga should be understood as worshipful for householders;
if the linga itself is greater, then it is worshipful for those who are indifferent (ascetics).
Regarding the term *kiṃvadantī*, see the section on characteristics (*lakṣaṇakāṇḍa*) contained in Hemādri’s work.
In the Sūtasamhitā, however:
When weighed seven times on a scale, it increases in weight and does not decrease;
such is the Vāṇaliṅga when meditated upon, while the remainder is said to be Nārmmada.
That which does not achieve equilibrium on the scale even three times five (fifteen) times is [of another kind].
At that time, it was declared that the arrow was made of reeds, while the remainder was produced from stone.
In the Vīramitrodaya.
Or when it is thrown back again into the river and is subsequently recovered, know that to be a *vāṇaliṅga*; though small in size, it increases happiness.
Thus concludes the examination of the Bāṇa-liṅga.
The etymological derivation of the word *vāṇa* is also found in that very same place.
Now, I shall explain from the beginning how Bāṇa is described:
the god Sadāśiva is Bāṇa, and there is also that which is within Bāṇa.
Because it was fashioned by him for him, it is therefore called the Bāṇaliṅga.
Śiva, the bestower of all goals, is eternally present there;
that Liṅga was installed by Śiva known as Bāṇa,
having the shape of a lotus fruit and the form of an earring.
"The lotus fruit is the seed of the lotus;
it has the appearance of a ripe jambu fruit and a shape like a hen's egg"— this is the reading in the *Lakṣaṇakāṇḍa* as cited in Hemādri.
The Bāṇaliṅga is declared to be the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In the Yājñavalkya-saṃhitā: Śiva’s words addressed to the Goddess.
A Liṅga from the Narmadā is praised when it has the shape of a ripe jambu fruit;
likewise, one that is honey-colored, white, blue, or with the luster of emerald is recommended.
Furthermore, for the purpose of installation, one shaped like a young swan is highly commended.
The Liṅga itself flows forth into the waters of the Narmadā from the mountain.
Formerly, on the bank of the Narmadā, I was requested by the Asura Bāṇa;
thus Maheśvara, in the form of a Liṅga, established his residence there upon that mountain.
Therefore, the Bāṇaliṅga is renowned on the surface of the earth;
whatever fruit a mortal might obtain from worshipping ten million other liṅgas,
that same fruit he obtains from the worship of a single Bāṇaliṅga.
Likewise.

A pedestal (vedikā) should be fashioned from copper, crystal, gold, stone, or silver; having established [the Liṅga] there, one should worship it. Whoever daily worships the Narmadā Liṅga with a spirit of devotion, [attains the supreme goal].
What worldly fruit does he have? Liberation is already held in his hand.
Thus concludes the fruit of the daily worship of the *vāṇaliṅga*.
In the Sūtasamhitā.
Having installed a Śrī-Vāṇaliṅga, its merit becomes ten million times that of [other] jewels. The fruit of a Rasaliṅga is remembered as being ten million times greater than that of a Vāṇaliṅga.
Only Śaṅkarī is able to describe the qualities of the Rasaliṅga.
The supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, are firmly established within the *rasaliṅga*.
In the Kedārakhaṇḍa.
Even though lingas made of precious gems have been described,
they too are indeed pure, worthy of worship, and bestowers of all desires.
Nevertheless, among all of these, that which is made of Kashmiri [saffron] is truly preeminent.
The Bāṇaliṅga is superior even to the Liṅga of Kāśmīra;
nothing more pure than the Bāṇaliṅga is seen here in this world.
It bestows everything pertaining to this life and the next upon the one who performs its worship.
Thus ends the praise of the Bāṇaliṅga.
He states the indicative mark of censure in that very same place:
If the *vāṇaliṅga* is rough, there will be the loss of sons and wife;
if that flattened one is worshipped, the destruction of the household will certainly occur;
if it leans to one side, there is the loss of cattle, sons, wife, and wealth.
If the arrow is broken at the head, there will be disease and even death;
if the arrow is worshipped with a perforated mark, there will be departure to a foreign land;
and if one sees a pericarp on the linga, the man becomes afflicted by disease.
If the tip of the banner is excessively high, there will be a loss of cattle wealth.
As recorded in the Hemādri.

One should avoid a [liṅga] that has a sharp tip, a curved head, or the characteristic of being triangular; likewise, one who is a householder should avoid one that is excessively thick, excessively thin, too small, or adorned with ornaments— for such things are beneficial for one seeking liberation.
Thus ends the definition of the characteristics of a defective *vāṇaliṅga*.
The auspicious signs are stated in the Vīramitrodaya:
A Kapila-liṅga that bestows wealth and resembles a dark cloud should be worshipped by those desiring liberation.
A householder should never, under any circumstances, worship a Kapila-liṅga that is small or large;
rather, it should be worshipped by a householder with one that has the color of a bee.
Whether it has a pedestal or no pedestal, and is devoid of mantra-consecration,
such a linga situated upon any pedestal of grace bestows both supernatural power (siddhi) and liberation (mukti).
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the Śubhavāṇa-linga.
The words of Bhairava in the Sūtasamhitā.
O blessed lady, in ancient times the Asura Vāṇa was exceedingly dear to Śiva;
he had conquered anger, was devoted, and was intent upon the rites of Śiva’s worship.
He was skilled in the science of fire, proficient in the arts, and endowed with auspicious marks.
Day after day, having personally offered [the materials] and installed the Liṅga, one should worship it.
Thus, O Goddess, one should worship for a hundred divine years.
Then Śaṅkara, who is easily attained through devotion to Him, became manifest before his eyes.
Śaṅkara said:
"I am pleased with you, O Vāṇa! Ask for a boon; what do you desire?
Hearing these words of Śaṅkara, Vāṇa spoke this speech:
"If you are indeed pleased with me, who am lowly and unfortunate..."
"I am afflicted, O Lord of Gods! Having fashioned your *liṅga* day after day—
its characteristics perfected according to those specific marks prescribed by the scriptures—
the meaning of the scriptures is difficult to attain, O God, and the successful accomplishment of that goal is likewise difficult to achieve."
Therefore, if you are pleased with me, grant me a well-characterized *liṅga* that fulfills all desires and shows compassion toward all beings;
for the sake of the welfare of all, O Śaṅkara, show me your grace!
Having heard these words of his, Śiva, the supreme cause,
caused fourteen crores of liṅgas to be fashioned by Śaṅkara upon the summit of Kailāsa.
Then that very Siddhaliṅga, which is eternally manifest by its own nature,
was offered by Bāṇa as a perfectly complete whole without any further application;
and Bāṇa, while being installed, bestows inexhaustible fruit perpetually.

Having worshipped him and shown affection with sincere devotion, the pure Vāṇa then led him to his own city; yet, even as he was being established there day after day, he reflected that it was insufficient,
for it would never become inexhaustible.
For the sake of the accomplishment of sentient beings,
three crores of lingas were gathered in the well-proportioned place of Vāṇa, at the cavity of Kālikā;
three crores at Śrīśaila, and one crore at Kanyakāśrama.
There is one crore at Māheśvara and one crore at Kanyātīrtha;
likewise, there is one crore each at Mahendra and in Nepāla.
Because the liṅga was fashioned for the purpose of Vāṇa’s worship, it is therefore known as the Vāṇaliṅga.
Or, since Śiva is said to be the arrow (*vāṇa*), that which is made by him is called *vāṇa*.
Therefore, in those regions or in those sacred places,
that true essence of Śiva resides within the physical form of Śiva’s icon.
The characteristic of its form is [to be made] of gold;
even when combined [with others], like a self-manifested linga (svayambhū-liṅga), a Bāṇa-linga leads to worldly enjoyment and one's own liberation.
It yields a thousandfold fruit compared to others when worshipped in its proper place.
On Śrīśaila, at Kālikāgarta, on Liṅgādri, at Kanyakāśrama,
at Kanyātīrtha, in the forest, at Yāna, at Mahendra, or at Sureśvara—
these Bāṇaliṅgas are situated, for they were indeed created by Śiva himself.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara, concerning the Bāṇaliṅgas:
At that time, however, even a pedestal of a different color may be of a single type;
it should be devoid of the *lakṣma* and the *mūrti*, and the arrow-shaped (*bāṇa*) [pedestal] should have a broad tip.
In the case of *bāṇaliṅgas*, rites such as invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth are not to be performed.
This has been stated in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa:
O Indra among kings! The Bāṇaliṅgas established throughout the three worlds require neither consecration nor ritual purification, nor even invocation.
In the fifth chapter of the *Yogasāra*.
Having risen during the *brāhma* muhūrta, whoever remembers the *bāṇaliṅga* attains victory everywhere; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvara!
Now, the meditation on the Bāṇaliṅga is described in that very same place.

Oṃ! [I bow to] the Great Lord named Vāṇa, who is heedless, endowed with power, called by the name Vāṇa, and possessed of great splendor; the God who is accompanied by the arrows of desire, capable of burning away the cycle of worldly existence, and radiant with the aesthetic sentiments beginning with the erotic.
Having meditated thus, one should worship that supreme Śiva as the arrow-liṅga;
having honored him mentally with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should recite his mantra.
Likewise:
Having then performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should satisfy the Bāṇaliṅga;
having meditated upon the identity of that with one's chosen deity, one should recite the Vāgbhava mantra.
Then, having completed the recitation, one should propitiate [the deity] with this hymn.
Now follows the hymn of praise.
Oṃ, O Bāṇaliṅga! O illustrious one! O Lord, protect me from saṃsāra!
Salutations to you of fierce form; salutations to you whose source is manifest! Salutations to you, the creator of saṃsāra; salutations to you who bear a subtle form!
Salutations indeed to the heedless Mahendra, who is the embodiment of Time!
Salutations to you, the burner; salutations to you, the performer of yoga.
Salutations again and again to the creator of enjoyment for those who possess it, and to the bestower of liberation.
Salutations to the destroyer of Kama’s body; salutations to the remover of impurity;
salutations to the giver of the universe and salutations to the one whose nature is the universe;
salutations to the granter of boons to Vana and to the destroyer of Ravana.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon Rāma, for the kingdom of Bharata,
for the giver of yoga to the sages, and for the destruction of the rākṣasas—
salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations to you, salutations again and again.
Aiṃ! To the one endowed with the burning power (dāhikā-śakti), to the beloved of Mahāmāyā,
to the beloved of Bhaga, to the All-pervading One, to the subduer of enemies, to the protector of yogins, and to the beloved of the Kaulikas.

Salutations to Nārāyaṇa, who is devoted to noble women, who delights in the conduct of the virtuous, and who is the yoga for those devoted to their lineage; salutations again and again to the Lord of Yoga,
who is intoxicated by the drinking of honey-wine.
For the destruction of the reproach against the family and for the happiness of the Kaulikas;
for the sake of the Kula-yoga, for the ultimate goal, for the pure Supreme Self;
for that which is the very nature of the Supreme Self and whose essence is the root of the Liṅga.
"To the Lord of All, to the All, to Śiva, and to the One Beyond Attributes"—O Śaṅkara! this is the supreme secret of the Vāṇaliṅga.
That best of practitioners who recites this shall attain the status of a Gaṇapati.
By the grace of this hymn, a yogi shall attain the state of a yogi;
for those desiring a kingdom, there shall be a kingdom, and for those seeking enjoyments, there shall indeed be enjoyment.
O God! For the virtuous, it shall be their spiritual practice, and for the Kaulikas, it shall become their Kula.
Whatever the practitioner of mantra desires, he obtains that with ease;
by the grace of the Vāṇaliṅga, he attains everything quickly.
What more need I say here? You know it all, O Lord of the Kula!
O Lord of the family! when great fear has arisen at the royal gate,
when danger from another country has arrived, or when there is a tumult of bandits, thieves, and the like,
one never encounters fear anywhere by reciting this King of Hymns.
I have briefly related the majesty of the Bāṇaliṅga;
by merely hearing of it, a person shall attain liberation.
The Bāṇaliṅga is to be constantly worshipped by yogis in their practice of yoga.
Whether it be the Kula-observance of the Kaulikas, the battle against enemies by the Paśus,
the recitation of the Vedas by those who know the Vedas, or the destruction of disease by the sick—
if anyone does not worship Him, all of that shall become fruitless.
Thus ends the hymn to the Bāṇaliṅga in the *Śrīyogasāra*, the supreme of all Āgamas, within the dialogue between Pārvatī and Śiva.
Now follows the definition of the Raudra-liṅga.
As held in the Vīramitrodaya.
The "fierce" (raudra) [fire] originates from a river through the mutual friction [of its banks];
it is called fierce because it arises simultaneously with the force of the river's current and is oily.
This also applies to the case of accumulation.
The form of the Raudra-liṅga, which brings happiness, should be understood as having the configuration of a river's current and the shape of a Bāṇa-liṅga; likewise, the form of the Narmadā,
the essence of rivers, is like that of a Bāṇa-liṅga.
Other types of *liṅgas* should also be understood as being *raudra* (fierce). The *raudra-liṅga* is likewise known to have the same form as the *vāṇa-liṅga*.
White, red, yellow, and black are worshipped by the Brahmins and the other [castes], respectively.
"By its very nature it is black in color and grants success among all castes;
born from the Narmadā river, it is fierce and is said to be like a Bāṇaliṅga."
Thus ends the definition of the Raudra-liṅga. || 1 ||
Now follows the definition of the Śivanābhi.
In the dialogue between Śiva and Nārada cited in the Vīramitrodaya, concerning the Śiva-liṅga:
The *liṅga* is said to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior.
That which is four finger-breadths in height and possesses a beautiful pedestal is declared by the sages learned in the scriptures to be the superior *liṅga*.
Half of that is declared the middling [measure], and half of that is remembered as the lowest;
its greatness is also described in that very same place.
Having worshipped the Liṅga consisting of the navel of Śiva, which is the most excellent of all Liṅgas by the great sages, it should therefore be worshipped according to the prescribed rite.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the Śivanābhi-linga. || 2 ||
Now, the characteristics of the divine linga.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara.
A liṅga that has the touch of cupped palms, is adorned with a trident, a chisel, and a crescent moon,
is provided with lines and hollows, possesses elevations and depressions, is elongated in shape, and is devoid of the Brahma-portion and other such divisions— [is to be known as the Śiva-liṅga].

The *liṅga* is said to be the *gola*; now the *golaka* is being described. Shaped like the fruit of the *kuṣmāṇḍa*, resembling the fruit of the *nāgaraṅga*, and shaped like the fruit of the *kākaḍimba*—this is declared to be the *golaliṅga*.
Thus ends the definition of the *golaliṅga*.
Now follows the definition of the characteristics of an Ṛṣi-liṅga.
In that very same [text].
The transformation of the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) takes on the forms of various bilva fruits;
that liṅga which is thick at its base, resembling a wood-apple (*kapittha*) fruit,
or which has the shape of a lotus stalk and is thick in the middle.
In the middle, the excellent thick liṅga is declared to be Ṛṣivāṇa.
Thus ends the definition of the characteristics of the *ārṣa* [type of] *liṅga*. || 5 ||
Now, the characteristics of the liṅga.
For the linga is of two kinds: non-artificial and artificial.
The non-artificial (*akṛtrima*) consists of self-manifested (*svayambhūta*) lingas of stone and so forth;
the artificial (*kṛtrima*) consists of those fashioned (*nirmita*), such as lingas made of metal elements (*dhātu*).
This is stated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*.

Having bowed to Nārada, Ārya, and the others, as well as the Liṅga in the form of a flour-mass and a water-drop, and Brāhmī in the form of a stone and an earthen mold, I shall describe the characteristics of the Liṅga.
That Liṅga should be known to be of two kinds: immovable and movable.
Each of these should be known as threefold, including that which possesses the nature of both.
A linga installed in a temple is immovable, being produced from stone or other materials. A linga installed at home is immovable, being fixed and stable.
That linga exists in five ways: the self-manifested (svayambhū), the divine (daiva), the protected (pālaka), the rishi-made (ārṣa), and the mental (mānasa); their characteristics are now described.
In the *Dīpikā*:
"To the teacher-muni, Maheśvara became manifest of his own accord;
and where the linga is self-manifested, let that be *svayambhū*."
Through contact with the *dhamanī*, it indeed burns very quickly;
that very channel, distinct from the *suṣumnā*, *iḍā*, and *piṅgalā*, pierces the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and ascends.
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*.
That linga which is seen on the earth as being well-endowed with various apertures, possessed of various colors, having its base unseen, and being hard,
is a self-manifested (svayambhūta) linga, distinct from others and free from [artificial] characteristics.
That which is called the *svayambhū-liṅga* is considered to be of various kinds:
the *liṅga* with a head resembling a conch shell is declared to be Vaiṣṇava;
that with a head resembling a lotus is Brāhma; and that with a head resembling an umbrella is said to be Śākra.
The pair of heads is said to belong to Agni; the three-footed form is assigned to Yama.
The sword-like Liṅga belongs to Nairṛta, while the one shaped like a water-pot (kalaśa) belongs to Varuṇa.
The banner-like Liṅga is for Vāyu, and that endowed with a mace (gadā) is for Kubera.

That which has the appearance of Īśāna’s trident and has issued forth from the world-protectors and others is declared by those expert in all the scriptures to be the *svayambhū* (self-manifested) *liṅga*.
Thus ends the description of the characteristics of the self-manifested linga (svayambhūliṅga).
In the Matsya-sūkta.
O Pārvatī! Having beheld the self-manifested Liṅga of Maheśa, one is liberated from all sins and merges into the supreme Brahman.
The fruit of making offerings to these is described in that very same place.
Specifically, a stone linga leads to liberation, while worldly enjoyment follows as a secondary result;
an earthen linga is recommended for worldly enjoyment, while liberation follows as a secondary result.
Likewise, one should know that a wooden linga and a marked (cihna) linga function in the same way.
It should be known that a golden [image] bestows stable prosperity and grants sovereignty;
one made of copper increases progeny, while one of lead prolongs life.
The Padma Purāṇa.
Mercury (pārada) leads to great prosperity, and pearl to good fortune;
moonstone (candrakānta) is the conqueror of death, and gold (hāṭaka) grants all desires.
This is also stated in the *Kalpottara* as cited in the *Vīramitrodaya*.

The earth bestows all fruits, and the jewels are likewise; indeed, eight jewels beginning with Ananta are recorded, blazing like lightning. They provide illumination at night and act as destroyers of all poisons and the like.
The various types [of lingas] are to be distinguished by their colors, tastes, fragrances, and forms;
those made of diamond and the like, as well as crystal and the like, or fashioned from molasses, food, and so forth,
are considered to be temporary lingas that grant all desires to men.
In the Compendium of Characteristics.
The fragrant Liṅga bestows good fortune, while the floral Liṅga grants liberation.
Likewise:
A linga originating from various living beings bestows various desires;
a linga made of sand grants virtues; and a linga made of salt brings good fortune.

For the purpose of eradication (uccāṭana), one should worship with devotion that which is obtained from the noose (pāśa), which is the primary [mantra] bringing about the destruction of enemies; having performed it, one becomes temporarily impoverished.
In the Garuḍa Purāṇa.
Two parts of musk, four parts of sandalwood,
three parts of saffron, and four parts of camphor—
having prepared this "fourfold" fragrant emblem (*gandhaliṅga*) and having worshipped it with devotion, [one attains the desired fruit].
A man, together with his kinsmen, attains union with Śiva.
By fashioning a linga made of flowers and anointed with the scent of horses,
one shall enjoy the earth divided into nine regions and become a lord of the Gaṇas.
Whoever worships with devotion a linga fashioned from dust shall attain the station of a Vidyadhara and subsequently become equal to Shiva.
One desiring prosperity should fashion a linga of clay and worship it with devotion.
One should fashion [the objects] from pure cow dung— meaning, pure, free from contact with the ground, and collected from an empty place—
the ritual sequence of the staff (*yaṣṭikrama*), and the *liṅga* made from barley, wheat, or rice.
One who desires prosperity, one who desires nourishment, and one who desires a son should worship him.
A linga made of white sugar should be fashioned to increase health.
For the purpose of subjugation, a linga made of salt mixed with the three pungent spices (tālatrikaṭuka) should be used.
*Tāla* means yellow orpiment (*haritāla*).
Trikatu consists of ginger, long pepper, and black pepper as is well known.
Having worshipped the Linga made of cow's ghee, it increases the intellect.
Likewise:
with salt, one gains good fortune; with earth, one obtains all desires;
that produced from sesame paste grants wishes; and that produced from husks is prescribed for the purpose of killing.
Ash-born [ghee] bestows all fruits; molasses-born increases affection;
fragrance-born yields abundant qualities; sugar-born grants happiness;
bamboo-sprout-born promotes lineage; and cow-dung-born cures all diseases.
A *liṅga* produced from hair and bone destroys all enemies;
for the purposes of agitation (*kṣobhaṇa*) and killing (*māraṇa*), a *liṅga* produced from flour is supreme.
A *liṅga* produced from wood bestows poverty, while flour bestows the gift of eloquence (*sārasvata*).
A linga produced from curd or milk bestows fame, prosperity, and a pleasant countenance;
a linga born of grain grants grain; one arising from fruit shall grant fruit;
one originating from flowers leads to divine enjoyments, long life, and liberation; and one produced from the *dhātrī* fruit likewise does so.
A linga produced from fresh butter increases fame and good fortune;
one produced from a blade of dūrvā grass wards off untimely death;
and a linga originating from camphor bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The magnet is to be known as fourfold in the context of common accomplishments.
There is a specific distinction in the *Sārasaṃgraha*.
Not every kind of gem is supreme; among them, the diamond (vajra) is for cutting enemies.
The twin-liṅga (yamaliṅga) is for great prosperity, and the pearl (mauktika) is for good fortune.
The great sapphire (mahānīla) is the root of nourishment, while the one originating from the Tīrasa river is for [attaining] light.
A touchstone made of fire-glass (taijasa), produced from sun-crystal (sūryakānta), serves for the prosperity of one's family;
a crystal [touchstone] known as Candrāpīḍa conquers death and grants all desires.
"Candrāpīḍa" means "moon-loved," that is to say, moonstone.
Likewise, there is the pearl produced from the gem known as *śūla* for the purpose of destroying enemies;
that is the *śūlamaṇi*, by whose presence the disease of colic (*śūlaroga*) is destroyed.
A diamond should be known as removing poverty; a pearl from its source removes disease;
a large one acquired at a sacred ford brings auspiciousness; lapis lazuli destroys the pride of enemies;
sapphire should be known as bestowing prosperity; and crystal grants all desires.
In the Kālottara [Tantra].
The golden [image] bestows great prosperity, while the silver one increases fortune;
likewise, the brass and bell-metal ones grant liberation equally to all—listen to this.
Ārakūṭa is brass.
A phallic emblem made of trapusa and iron is beneficial for the destruction of enemies.
Likewise:
a linga made of bell-metal bestows fame; one made of silver increases progeny;
one made of copper is for the sake of enjoyment and liberation; and one made of mixed metals grants all perfections.
It is composed of eight elements produced from a mixture.
In the dialogue between Śiva and Nārada.
A man should worship a linga made of silver for the liberation of his ancestors;
he should worship one made of gold to attain Satyaloka;
indeed, a human being desiring prosperity should worship a linga made of copper.
The worship of liṅgas made of copper and other materials, however, pertains to periods other than the Kali age;
as it is stated in the Matsyasūkta:
In the Kali age, one should not worship a linga made of copper, nor one of brass or lead;
likewise, a linga of red sandalwood, conch-shell, bell-metal, or iron.
However, one who desires constant satisfaction should worship a linga made of bell-metal (pittala).
One who desires fame should always worship a linga made of bell-metal; one who desires the destruction of enemies should always worship a linga made of iron;
and a man desiring long life should always worship a linga made of lead.
Also in the *Lakṣaṇasamuccaya*:
"An image made of gold bestows stable fortune; one of silver grants sovereignty;
one of brass increases progeny; and one of copper increases longevity."
Bell-metal causes enmity, while that made of brass destroys enemies.
Rītija means made of brass.
A linga made of lead destroys diseases; one made of iron destroys enemies;
a linga made of the eight metals (aṣṭaloha) brings about the destruction of leprosy and consumption;
and a linga produced from the three metals (triloha) bestows perfection regarding spiritual knowledge.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
The linga born of vajra bestows prosperity; that born of śilājatu grants all supernatural powers (siddhis);
that born of minerals directly bestows wealth; and that born of wood grants the attainment of enjoyments.
In the Kālottara [Tantra].
One who desires wealth should worship a linga made of fragrant flowers, as well as one fashioned from food and other such substances; one who desires beauty should worship a linga produced from musk;
and one who desires a beautiful form should worship a linga originating from gorocana.
One who desires beauty should always wear a linga made from saffron;
one made from white agalloch increases great intelligence,
while a linga produced from black agalloch bestows the power of concentration (dhāraṇā).
And in the twelfth chapter of the Mātṛkābhedatantra.
In the worship of Śiva using an earthen image, one shall be endowed with all perfections (siddhis).
In the worship of Śiva using a stone image, it is taught that the fruit is twofold.
And in the worship of a golden liṅga, the destruction of enemies is considered the result.
The Lord of all Siddhis [is attained] through silver; from that, the fruit is fourfold.
One should know that nourishment comes through copper, while there is loss of wealth through bell-metal.
In the Gaṅgā it is a hundred-thousandfold, and through lac one becomes afflicted by disease.
O Dear One! Through a crystal [liṅga] there shall be all success, and likewise through an emerald;

through an iron liṅga there is the destruction of enemies, while the ash liṅga grants desires. Through sand there is the accomplishment of desired objects, and through cow dung there is the slaying of enemies.
The majesty of the Sarvalinga bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa.
In the Śivadharmottara, as cited in the Ṣaṭkarmadīpikā:
Brahmā constantly worships an auspicious linga made of stone;
by worshipping it, he attained supreme Brahman-hood.
Viṣṇu always worships a linga made of sapphire.
By that [merit], he attained the state of Viṣṇu and became the sole protector of all beings.
Varuṇa always worships a crystal linga that is stainless;
by that, he indeed attained the status of Varuṇa, endowed with splendor and strength.
Also in the seventh chapter of the Mātṛkābhedatantra:
One should worship [the Lord] in an earthen liṅga, or in a stone liṅga;
O Goddess, or in a liṅga of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal;
or in mercury, or in the Gaṅgā, or even in crystal or emerald.
One may worship in a linga made of metal for specific purposes, or in a linga fashioned from ash,
or in a linga made of sand, or even in one made of cow dung; O Goddess, however, one should not worship in a linga made of stone without the performance of the purificatory rites (saṃskāra).
Thus end the materials for the manufacture of the Śivaliṅga.
Now follows the consecration of the Śiva-liṅga.
In that very same [text].
I shall now describe the ritual procedure (saṃskāra) and whatever specific details may apply here: having placed a silver or golden liṅga in a golden vessel,
one should lift that liṅga out of it and submerge it in milk for three days.
Having bathed [the deity] with Tryambaka, one should worship Kālarudra;
on the altar, one should worship Pārvatī with the sixteen-fold service (ṣoḍaśopacāra).
Then, having lifted that liṅga from there, [one should immerse it] in the waters of the Gaṅgā for three days.
Then, the wise person should perform the consecration according to the procedure prescribed in the Vedas.
By the previously cited statements, worship of various kinds of *liṅgas* has been taught for the sake of specific desired fruits.
And that worship is as follows: "One should fashion a *liṅga* with auspicious characteristics and discard a *liṅga* that lacks such characteristics."
If the length is deficient, disease will arise; if it is excessive, there will be an increase in enemies.
If the measurement is deficient, destruction will occur; if it is excessive, there will be the loss of children.
If the width is either excessive or deficient, the ruin of the kingdom will certainly occur.
If it lacks a pedestal, there is poverty; if it lacks a head, there is the destruction of the lineage;
and if it lacks the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), the kingdom of kings perishes.
Therefore, with every effort, one should fashion a linga endowed with auspicious characteristics.
By such statements as these, it is declared that only the *liṅga* possessing auspicious characteristics (*sulakṣaṇa*) is the bestower of fruit.
This is stated in the second chapter of the *Liṅgārcana-tantra*.
The Goddess said:
The god Sadāśiva is devoid of sense organs and is of the nature of emptiness;
there is no form of the god—what, then, is the fruit of his worship?
Śiva said:
O Maheśānī! O Pārvatī! there is never any worship of the Pretas. O Parameśānī! Rudra’s power is declared to be Raudrī;
and that Raudrī, O Parameśānī, is the primordial Kuṇḍalinī.
O Supreme Śānī! She exists as the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
encircling Śiva, she remains forever in the form of three and a half coils.
O Maheśānī! Without Śakti, his state as a ghost (preta) is certain.
By the mere union with Śakti, Sadāśiva becomes the agent of action;
for this very reason, O Maheśānī, one should worship the Śivaliṅga.
Thus concludes the fruit of worshipping the Śiva-liṅga together with the Śakti.
In the Mātṛkātantra, in the seventh chapter.
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods! O Master! Tell me about the authoritative characteristics of the linga;
and whatever specific distinction there may be regarding those made of earth, stone, and other materials.
The illustrious Śiva said:
One *tolaka* of clay should be taken, or perhaps two *tolakas*;
one should never do otherwise than this, O Pārvatī!
Also in the Viśvasāra-tantra, as cited in the Ṣaṭkarmadīpikā:
One should take one *tolaka* or two *tolakas* of clay;
the wise man should have it fashioned according to the measurement of three threads.
Having made the *liṅga* the size of one's own thumb-joint, one should worship it.
The means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for fashioning the linga out of clay and other materials has been proclaimed;
the fruit is said to be attained [thereby], but if it is otherwise, then the result is otherwise. The method of the three-threaded ritual (*trisūtrīkaraṇa*) is taught in the *Kālottara*.
By the application of equal lines upon the *liṅga*, the altar (*vedī*), and likewise the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should understand them to be level;
this is the process of establishing the three lines.
In that regard, according to the different types of clay, there is a difference in the fruit of the worship for the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes.
Praiseworthiness has been stated.
In the third chapter of the Liṅgārcana Tantra.
O Pārvatī, the earthen *liṅga* is of four kinds according to the varieties of clay:
white, red, yellow, and black, O Supreme Goddess!
White is recommended for a Brāhmaṇa, while red is desired for a Kṣatriya.
Yellow indeed belongs to the Vaiśya caste, while black is proclaimed for the Śūdra;
likewise:

O Supreme Goddess! he who fashions a white earthen linga and worships it shall indeed become a partaker of the fruits of the three goals of life. O lady of excellent hips! a Kshatriya, however, having fashioned a red earthen [linga]...

He who constantly worships [this] shall obtain the fruit of the three aims of life (trivarga). O Goddess! he who, having fashioned a green earthen [image], worships it—he too, O Maheśānī, shall become a Vaiśya and partake in the fruit of the three aims of life.
O Supreme Goddess! That Śūdra who, having fashioned a black earthen linga, worships it, shall partake in the fruits of the three aims of life.
In the Mātṛkābhedatantra.
And on stone and other materials, O Maheśānī! it yields a gross fruit; on the measure of a thumb, O Deveśī! or on the scale of Mount Meru, O Devadeveśī! one shall obtain manifold fruits in due order.
O Supreme Goddess! The rudrākṣa is the most massive of all massive lingas.
O Goddess! It is recorded that manifold fruits result from its worship and wearing.
The phrase "the most massive of all massive" refers to something other than the earthen (pārthiva) linga.
This is because of the specific statement previously mentioned, "one *tolaka* of clay.
The method for fashioning the five-fold cord (*pañcasūtrī*) for stones such as crystal, emerald, and others is described in the *Laiṅga-purāṇa* as follows:
Whatever is the measurement of the Śiva-liṅga, that same measurement applies to the right and left [sides];
and whatever is the measurement of the tip of the yoni, it should be the same at the bottom as well.
In another tantra:
Whatever the width of the *liṅga*, its circumference should be the same.
The pedestal (*vedī*) should be twice the size of the *liṅga*, and the womb (*yoni*) should be measured at half of that.
One should never, under any circumstances, make it shorter than a thumb's breadth.
In the fashioning of Śiva from jewels and other materials, a specific measurement may arise as if by necessity.
The etymological derivation of the word *liṅga* is found in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"They say that space (*ākāśa*) is the *liṅga*, and the earth is its pedestal (*pīṭhikā*).
Because it is the abode (*ālaya*) of all the gods and because [all things] dissolve (*layana*) therein, it is called *liṅga*. (p. 629)
Śiva said:
I am not satisfied by being worshipped with flowers, incense, and offerings in an image;
likewise, O Pārvatī, I am supremely satisfied when the Liṅga is worshipped.
Thus, O Goddess, in former times during that ritual act, I was conquered by all the deities.
Because it is a sign (*liṅga*), it is called a *liṅga* by the gods, asuras, and kinnaras. "O Goddess! I grant heaven to whoever is devoted to the worship of my *liṅga*.
Having abandoned all sins, with his impurities burnt away, he shall go forth free from bondage."
With mind fixed on Me and offering salutations to Me, he attains Me alone;
even the fruit of worship and other rites, through the excellence of the material offered, resides in Him alone.
O best of beings, that man who bathes my Liṅga with water filtered through a cloth obtains the fruit of a hundred thousand horse-sacrifices; likewise,
by anointing the Liṅga with devotion using fragrant sandalwood paste.
He is anointed by celestial women with fragrant yakṣakardama unguents.
The fault of performing the worship of a *liṅga* and the fruit of that worship are found in that very same [text],
in the dialogue between Śiva and Nārada.
For that wretched and evil-minded person whose time passes constantly without the worship of the Liṅga, there shall be a great loss;
on one side are all gifts and various vows.
Holy fords, observances, and sacrifices are all on one side;
there is nothing other than the worship of the Liṅga in the four Vedas of old.
This alone is the well-ascertained conclusion of all the scriptures.
Having constantly worshipped this Linga, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation and wards off various calamities, a person shall attain union with Śiva,
having completely abandoned all other nets of ritual actions without exception.
With supreme devotion, the wise man alone should worship the Liṅga.
In the Matsyasūkta, the sixteenth chapter.
Thousands of horse-sacrifices and hundreds of Vājapeya sacrifices do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of worshipping Maheśa.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
What need is there for much speaking here? This entire world, both moving and unmoving, remains established here after having worshipped the Śivaliṅga; of this there is no doubt.
In the Mātṛkābhedatantra:
O Goddess! By worshipping Śiva, one becomes the master of the four aims of life;
by worshipping Lord Śambhu, a mortal becomes endowed with the eightfold sovereign powers.
It is said that even Nārāyaṇa himself becomes so if he should worship Śambhu.
O Goddess! The worship of all those deities who eternally reside in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld becomes accomplished through the worship of Śambhunātha.
The words of Nārada from the Kālottara, as cited in the Ṣaṭkarmadīpikā.
In this truly essence-less cycle of existence, these four alone are the essence:
dwelling in Kāśī, association with the virtuous, the waters of the Gaṅgā, and the worship of Śambhu.
In the Skanda Purāṇa.
The Agnihotra sacrifices, the three Vedas, and sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees—
These are not equal to even a ten-millionth part of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga.
Having cut through and pierced all beings, and having abandoned this entire world, one should worship the god Virūpākṣa; he is not tainted by sin.
Wandering through thousands of various births over many thousands of lifetimes,
what man indeed attains liberation without the worship of the Liṅga?
In the Skanda Purāṇa as cited in the Vīramitrodaya.

A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra born of the natural order (anuloma) should constantly worship the Liṅga with devotion using their respective mantras. The phrase "using their respective mantras" means, as appropriate, by means of Vedic, Tantric, or name-mantras.
In the Liṅga Purāṇa:
At the base is Brahmā, and likewise in the middle is Viṣṇu, the lord of the three worlds;
above Rudra is Mahādeva, the eternal Śiva known as Praṇava.
The Veda is the Liṅga, and the Great Goddess is the Liṅga; Maheśvara is manifestly present.
By the constant worship of those two, both the altar and the deity are worshipped.
Now begins the majesty of the mercury-Śiva-liṅga.
In the eighth chapter of the Mātṛkābhedatantra.
O beloved! In the city of Kailāsa resides the great Liṅga composed of light;
a single sixteenth part of that very same [Liṅga] is Viśveśvara, situated in Kāśī.
O Maheśānī! This is the full Liṅga, the seed of Śiva, and not otherwise.
Just as the supreme Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa exists as a wheel within a stone,
so too there is not even a hundredth part of a mercury (pārada) that is Lakṣmī-Nārāyaṇa;
for the letter *pa* is the form of Viṣṇu, and the letter *ā* is Kālikā herself.
The letter *repha* is Śiva and the letter *da* is the form of Brahmā; it is not otherwise.
O Supreme Goddess! Mercury (*pārada*) consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
He who worships the mercury-liṅga is indeed the imperishable Sambhu himself.

O Goddess! O Queen of the Gods! He who worships even once during his lifetime is indeed blessed; he is a man of knowledge, a knower of reality, a knower of Brahman, wealthy, and is honored as a king upon this earth.
The supreme practitioner is the lord of the supernatural powers, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
Now follows the procedure for the manufacture of a mercury Śivaliṅga.
In that very same [text].

O Beloved! Since various obstacles arise during the preparation of mercury (pārada), which is the seed of Śiva, one should therefore perform rites for peace and prosperity (svastyayana), O Maheśānī! For mercury is indeed the seed of Śiva; one must certainly not subject it to heating (ṭāḍana).
From striking [the deity], there shall be loss of wealth; from striking, poverty;
from striking, affliction by disease; and from striking, death may occur.
One should worship the earthen linga in the twelfth [year] with the sixteen types of offerings.
One should offer a pair of garments, either white or fashioned from threads such as silk, according to what is appropriate for the person;
O Mistress of the Kula, the *madhuparka* fit for enjoyment should also be presented.
One should give ornaments according to one's ability for the sake of auspiciousness.
O Pārvatī! One should worship with great effort using bilva leaves;
according to the rite spoken by Toḍala, one should recite the mantra ten thousand times for each [leaf].
First, one should recite the five-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times. At the conclusion of the worship, one should subsequently recite the great mantra known as Prasāda.
Having performed the rites up to the final sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), one should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya) with the senses subdued.
One should never avoid betel-leaf and fish;
in this tantra, sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), betel-leaf,
and excellent fish should be offered in the fire-oblation (homa), O Supreme Goddess!— either in the tenth part or the hundredth part [of the total].
A sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the oblation should be given; then one is no longer tainted by obstacles.
Thereafter, on the following day, the wise practitioner should bring forth mercury (pārada).
Over that, he should recite the ninefold mantra which binds all things.

O Dear One! O Maheśānī! One should mutter this mantra over the medicinal herb: the seed-syllable of space (haṃ), the letter of Śiva (sa), preceded by a letter and topped with a bindu (hsaḥ), and the seed-syllable of wind (ya) joined with the moon (u)—this triad is Tryambaka.

If one recites the mantra one hundred and eight times over mercury, then by means of the application of the medicinal herbs it becomes bound; not otherwise. Listen, O beloved of my life! regarding what happens on the following day.
One should restrain the performer of all [rites] according to the extent of one's stated wealth.
One should place gold in the shape of a *campaka* flower upon the pair of ears;
and a beautiful, four-cornered piece of gold upon the neck.
O Maheśānī! One should offer a pair of bracelets upon both hands;
likewise, a bracelet of white color and a ring as well.
O Śivā! One should give a yellow-colored armlet and a pair of silken garments.
The wave is the ring.
Having done this, O Maheśānī! one should contemplate the form of Śiva.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual procedure; listen, O Pārvatī!
Having placed it upon a bed of grass and stirred it with the juice of *jhiṇṭī* leaves while reciting the *praṇava*, one should make it into a paste-like consistency, O Beloved!
If that substance is suitable for the construction, O beautiful goddess!
Then, having fashioned that linga, one should make it even more firm.
It should be placed upon a cloth joined with *khapuṣpa* (sky-flowers), and upon charcoal and cow-dung ash;
it should be made slightly warm so that it becomes very firm.
It is said regarding the Avadhūta: "One should shave the head; one should eat from a broken vessel; one should wear a patched garment;
one should carry a begging bowl; one should wander as a mendicant; indeed, this is the supreme state, the creation of Śiva."
O Cme, know that the hand of Jaḍaka has a vajra-like grip.
Thus concludes the procedure for the manufacture of the mercury-Śiva-liṅga.
The origin of the Śivaliṅga is described in the first chapter of the third *rātra* of the *Nāradapañcarātra*,
in the dialogue between Nārada and Brahmā, as follows:
Brahmā said:
Formerly, knowing you to be fickle, this was not revealed in your presence;
now, having known [this] from the yogis, I speak it—of this there is no doubt.
It is extremely secret, most secret, and exceedingly secret; of this there is no doubt.
It must be guarded, it must be guarded, it must be guarded by you as well.
It was concealed by Śambhu in this tantra, yet revealed in another tantra.
Listen, I shall tell it today; attend with full attention.
O Nārada! Indeed, at the beginning of creation, various creations were fashioned by me:
gods, dānavas, daityas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas—all these excellent beings are under the sway of women; progeny is born from sexual union.
Indeed, Śiva, the Auspicious One,
never set his mind upon the act of taking a wife, even after seeing the gods overcome with anxiety;
thus the gods, asuras, and others, including Indra, sought refuge in me alone.
Having prostrated and offered praise, they stood before him with concentrated minds;
with palms joined in reverence, they all spoke with voices faltering from fear.
The gods and others said:
We have all been married, as has even Janārdana;
yet Mahādeva alone—the God of gods and Lord of the universe—has not set his mind upon marriage. By whom, indeed, can Śiva be deluded?

"O All-pervading Lord! Devise a means so that the Lord may be accompanied by a wife, whereby he may become the protector of the worlds; perform that, O Treasure of Compassion! Having heard these words of theirs, Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures, then [acted].
Accompanied by them, the lotus-seated Brahmā went to Viṣṇu, the Lord of the World, who was mounted upon Garuḍa; he then spoke to that lotus-eyed one.
Brahmā said:
"O best of gods! I have created all human beings born of sexual union; yet, with the exception of Śambhu, they are all female. Tell me what must be done."
The Blessed One said:
"O mighty-armed one! Accompanied by these, you and I shall go for our welfare.
Having been duly authorized, he has indicated what must be done;
however, please arrange a suitable woman for him in marriage."
Brahmā said:
"Let us all go to Dakṣa; O Hari, grant him permission!
Let her quickly propitiate the primordial power, Mahāmāyā.
Having become a maiden, she will delude the great Śambhu, Śaṅkara."
Having spoken thus, Vidhi and Keśava went to where the highly effulgent Dakṣa was; they informed him of their purpose,
and the Lord of Creatures spoke appropriately to Dakṣa regarding the performance of penance.

Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and all of them propitiated Śivā through their austerity. That goddess Kālikā, the mistress of the mace, appeared and said to me: "O gods and asuras, for what purpose are you so full of longing?"
The Goddess said:
"Swiftly, according to your desire, I shall bestow the fruit of your prayer;
I shall grant it before long—this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt."
The gods and others said:
"Having become the daughter of Dakṣa, delude Śaṅkara!
O ever-auspicious one, fulfill this desire of ours and grant us success!
Having heard these words of theirs and having looked toward the lotus-seated Brahmā, [she replied:]
Overcome by [this], she spoke: "I am Kālikā, the Sovereign of the World."
The Goddess said:
"Śambhu is but a child today; how will he satisfy me? You are indeed a man worthy of me; therefore, provide another one."
Brahmā said:
Śambhu, the god who is the teacher of all, is indeed our supreme lord;
he, possessed of great courage and great splendor, will grant you satisfaction.
There is no man equal to Śambhu anywhere at any time.
Thus addressed by Brahmā, the Goddess, the Sovereign, spoke these words:
"Having granted Dakṣa the sight [of me], let a boon be requested.
Dakṣa, too, beheld that supreme Goddess, who held a sword and a chisel.
Dwarfed, with a protruding belly, her waist encircled by a tiger skin,
her two hands adorned with blue lotuses and a skull-cup, and bestowing boons— seeing her,
Dakṣa Prajāpati felt as though he had already accomplished his purpose.
Dakṣa said:
"If you are the granter of boons to me, even regarding that which is desired by the gods,
then, having become my daughter, do indeed delude Śaṅkara.
Having said, "So be it," the Mother of the World then vanished from sight.
Then, having bowed to the deities, the gods, accompanied by their wives, approached Hara— the Supreme Self and Lord of the World— where he was performing austerities.
They prostrated before him and praised him with devotion, speaking with voices faltering with emotion.
The gods and others said:
O Blessed One! O Lord of the gods of gods! O Protector of the worlds! O Great-souled One!
We all, together with our wives, are here for the sake of creation, O Supreme Lord;
therefore, please perform the marriage so that the protection of creation may be ensured.
In the house of Dakṣa, Mahākālī was proclaimed as Māyā;
she has been born for your pleasure, O Śambhu! She is certainly worthy of you, without a doubt.
The Lord said:
"I shall duly act for your pleasure; there is no doubt in this. Let preparations be made quickly for my marriage indeed.
Thus were all the gods addressed by the high-souled Lord.
Having accomplished their purpose, they all returned to their most beautiful abode and related to Dakṣa the words spoken by Śaṅkara;
then, having completed the marriage, they departed as they had come, their task fulfilled.

Then all departed, and Maheśa, together with Satī, went to his home; with a mind full of intense joy, he sported with Satī for a long time. Then, after some time had passed, Maheśvara was once again with Satī.
She was unable to carry it; being exhausted, Satī then spoke with a piteous voice to the God of gods, the Teacher of the World:
"O Blessed One, I am indeed unable to bear this burden of yours, which is so difficult to endure."
"Forgive me, O Mahādeva! Have mercy, O Lord of the World!
Having heard her words, the Blessed One whose banner is the bull, his mind intent on passion, engaged in intense and deep union with her.
Having completed their full union, the virtuous woman, though having abandoned sexual intercourse,
set her mind on rising; the supreme splendor of both fell upon the surface of the earth, pervading the entire world with those rays.
Then, in the netherworld (pātāla), on the earth (bhūtala), and in heaven (svarga), there were Śiva-liṅgas.
Therefore, all beings of the past and the future, along with their wombs (yonis), are Śiva-liṅgas.
Wherever there is a liṅga, there is a womb; wherever there is a womb, there is Śiva.
And from the splendors of both, the Śivaliṅga was born.
Thus ends the account of the origin of the Śivaliṅga.
It is stated in the sixty-fourth chapter of the Utpattitantra that everyone has the right to perform the worship of the Śivaliṅga.
Whether one is a Śākta, a Vaiṣṇava, a Saura, or a Gāṇapa, O Dear One, how can there be success for one who is devoid of the worship of Śiva?
And, O Goddess, he who worships another deity without having propitiated me—

O Great Goddess! He does not accept it; having uttered a curse, he shall depart for his city. O Goddess! Indeed, by means of sweet foods and the like, there are fruits as abundant as the mountain peaks and flowers according to the prescribed rite.

O Maheśvarī! Even if there were food of various kinds equal to Mount Sumeru, O Maheśānī! and even if the soup and other accompaniments were like the ocean—if such flowers and food offerings are given [to others], they all become nothing but excrement.
He who, devoid of the worship of Śiva, worships another deity—
especially in the Kali Yuga— that man shall become a partaker of sin.
This is also stated in the first chapter of the *Liṅgārcanatantre*.

O Queen of the Gods! Among all forms of worship, the worship of the Liṅga is the supreme state. O Goddess! For him who performs any other form of worship without the worship of the Liṅga, that worship shall be fruitless, and in the end he shall attain hell.

Therefore, O Maheśānī! one should first worship the Liṅga. O beloved! that kingdom which is constantly devoid of the worship of the Liṅga—I consider that kingdom fallen, remembered as being equal to a ground of excrement.

O Goddess! O Supreme Sovereign! if a Brāhmaṇa, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya does not worship the Liṅga, at that very moment all three shall become outcastes (Caṇḍālas). And a Śūdra, O Supreme Sovereign, shall always be like a pig.
O Goddess of gods! Know that house, O Pārvatī, in which the worship of Śiva is abandoned, to be equal to a pit of excrement, O Devī! In that dwelling, O Pārvatī, food is excrement and milk is urine.

O Supreme Goddess! O Fair-faced One! Whether one is a devotee of Śakti, Viṣṇu, or Śiva, having first worshipped the [original] Liṅga with bilva leaves, O Great Sovereign, one should thereafter pray to and worship another Liṅga.
Otherwise, O beloved, everything is like urine without the worship of Śiva.
In the Skanda Purāṇa, as cited in the Vīramitrodaya, concerning the Śiva-liṅga:
By seeing and by touching him, men obtain liberation;
yet it is not possible for me to describe his merit correctly even in hundreds of yugas according to the rules. Therefore, one should duly install that Śiva.
For all castes alike, the auspicious and divine form of the All-pervading Lord is well-constructed and worthy of contemplation;
yet for yogis, it is likewise beyond the reach of fruitive results.
He who, bypassing the Śiva-liṅga, should worship other deities—
That king, along with his kingdom, shall go to the Raurava hell.
All the gods beginning with Brahmā, kings together with the great sages,
as well as human beings and ascetics— all of them worship the Liṅga.
Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, having slain the son of Brahmā along with his army,
installed a Liṅga according to the prescribed rites with devotion on the bank of the lord of rivers;
even after committing thousands of sins and likewise killing hundreds of Brahmins.
One who takes refuge in the Liṅga is liberated from sin; there is no doubt about this.
All worlds consist of the Liṅga, and all are established in the Liṅga. Therefore, one should worship the Liṅga if one desires the eternal state.
The entire world consists of the *liṅga*; everything is established in the *liṅga*.
Therefore, with every effort, one should install and worship it.
Brahmā, Hara, the Lord, the Viśvedevas, Umā, and Hari [are all therein].
Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Smṛti, Prajñā, Vidhi, Durgā, and Śacī; likewise the Rudras, the Vasus, Skanda, Viśākha, Śākha,
the blessed Naigameśa, the world-protectors, and the planets.
All the Gaṇas led by Nandin, the Lord Gaṇapati, all the Pitṛs and Munis, the most excellent ones beginning with Kuvera,
the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, and the two Aśvins, the best of physicians;
All the gods, the assembled animals, birds, and wild beasts,
as well as everything from Brahmā down to the stationary world— all this is established in the Liṅga.
Therefore, with every effort, one should install the Īśvara-liṅga.
If a person should worship a linga installed by a servant, [he shall incur the following].
Also elsewhere.
The Lord Brahmā dwells at the base, Viṣṇu in the middle portion, and Śambhu Paśupati,
the stainless and most excellent form of Rudra,
is at the top; therefore, one should install or worship the Liṅga as the Guru, the celestial tree, because it is worthy of worship.

All the foremost of the gods constantly worship this Gaṇapati— who is praised by the best of the thirty deities— with fragrances, flowers, sweet scents, abundant offerings, hymns, mantras, and ritual services.

They worship Maheśa in his *liṅga* form; being free from fear regarding [the cycle] beginning with conception and ending in destruction, they are honored by the foremost of gods and gandharvas, revered by the Siddhas, saluted by the best of the Gaṇas, and they worship those immeasurable ones.
Therefore, one should install the Supreme Lord with devotion and service,
and especially worship the Liṅga for the attainment of all goals.
Likewise: "Therefore, Maheśvara in the form of the Liṅga should always be worshipped;
as long as there is worship of the Lord of the Gods, so long does one's residence remain in heaven."
Therefore, Śiva should be worshipped constantly by those endowed with faith.
The entire world consists of the *liṅga*, and everything is established within the *liṅga*.
For this reason, one who desires his own perfection should worship the *liṅga*.
By the worship of the Liṅga alone, all the gods, Daityas,
Dānavas, Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Siddhas, Rākṣasas,
and flesh-eaters have attained perfection after worshipping the form of the Liṅga; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O gods, one should always worship the Liṅga with whatever means possible!
Likewise:
"Those who desire great enjoyments or sovereignty in the abode of the thirty gods should always worship Maheśvara in the form of the Liṅga."
Having cut through and pierced all beings, and having destroyed this entire world, one may sacrifice to the single Virūpākṣa; he is not defiled by such vessels.
These are recorded in the Vīramitrodaya.
Now, the fruit of worshipping the liṅga at the three times of day.
In the Matsya Sūkta.
Whoever, having risen in the morning, should worship a *liṅga* anywhere with devotion,
shall obtain that fruit which comes from giving a hundred tawny cows (*kapilā*). Whoever should worship the *liṅga* when the midday sun has arrived, [shall likewise obtain great merit].
One shall obtain that fruit which is gained by giving away the entire earth.
Likewise.
One should worship Śiva one thousand and eight times every day, whether once a day or three times a day; such a person purifies three lineages.
O Goddess of gods! Or [one may worship] eight times eight, or a hundred, or even half of that.
One should know that everything— the thousandfold [merit] residing in the letter *ma*,
wealth, long life, women, sons, and whatever else is desired by the mind—
is attained by the sacrificer upon reaching a crystal linga.
Better is the abandonment of life or even the cutting off of one's head,
than that one should ever employ the Śivaliṅga, Maheśvara, without first having worshipped it.
Also in the Skanda Purāṇa, as cited in the Ṣaṭkarmadīpikā:
Whoever, having risen in the morning, should worship the Liṅga even once with devotion,
shall obtain that fruit which comes from the gift of a hundred thousand tawny cows.
Whoever should worship the Liṅga when the midday sun has arrived, [shall likewise obtain great merit].
Whoever worships Śiva when the sun has entered the constellation Vāruṇī shall obtain the fruit that is acquired by giving away the entire earth;
he shall obtain the fruit of having given a hundred thousand cows.
(p. 638) Now, regarding the number of earthen Śiva-liṅgas according to different desires, as recorded in the *Vīramitrodaya*:
"The number of earthen liṅgas is declared according to one's desire."
The earthen liṅga is known as *sṛlliṅga*; it is supreme for bestowing both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Having understood the proper place, time, and other factors, one should fashion a liṅga that yields fruit. If one does not act after having understood these requirements, the purpose of that undertaking will not be accomplished.
One seeking knowledge should perform it one hundred thousand times; one seeking wealth, half of that;
one seeking a son, one thousand five hundred; and one seeking a daughter, three hundred.
A learned man should perform ten thousand repetitions of the *liṅga*, which is the supreme remover of all sins.
One desiring sovereignty obtains a hundred thousand; one desiring a beloved woman, five hundred;
one desiring liberation, ten millionfold; one desiring prosperity, a thousand;
one desiring beauty, three thousand; and one desiring the power of sacred pilgrimage sites, two thousand.
One desiring friendship [should recite] one thousand; for the sake of clothing, one hundred and eight;
for the purpose of killing, seven hundred; for the purpose of deluding, one hundred and eight;
and for expulsion and subjugation, one thousand, as has been stated.
For the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*), one thousand [recitations] are prescribed; for killing (*māraṇa*), half of that.
In the event of fear of a great king or in times of calamity and distress, five hundred are required.
One thousand or ten thousand is proclaimed as the total for all [other] rites.
The single Liṅga is declared to be the remover of sin; the pair of Liṅgas bestows the accomplishment of wealth;
and the triad of Liṅgas is said to be the supreme cause for the fulfillment of all desires.
Likewise.
By making ten thousand *liṅgas* and performing worship, one removes the fear of kings;
by making thousands of *liṅgas*, one will certainly be released from shackles.
For the sake of liberation from prison, a wise person should have ten thousand made.
In case of fear from ḍākinīs and others, one should then perform five thousand [recitations];
and one who is childless should indeed cause fifty thousand to be performed.
Thus it is stated in the ninth chapter of the *Liṅgārccanatantra*.
And by this sequence, O Goddess! he who worships a hundred thousand [times] obtains the fruit of all his desires; there is no doubt in this matter, O Goddess!
Likewise.
O Maheśānī! one should not worship the pair by merging them together;
O Maheśānī! having merged the fifteen hundred [petals] together, or else, O Devī, one should worship with each individual bilva leaf.
One should worship each liṅga individually; one should not worship them as a pair.
O Goddess, by worshipping them as a pair, one becomes poor.
Thus ends the prohibition against the worship of the pair of *liṅgas*.
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Branches," in the fifth section on Devotion within the *Śrī-Prāṇatoṣiṇī*.
p. 639) Now follows the worship of Śiva.
In the Matsyasūkta Mahātantra, in the fifteenth chapter.
Having collected earth from a sacred bathing place (tīrtha) and fashioned a wonderful liṅga—O Maheśānī! in the absence of a tīrtha, O lady of pure smiles, [use] earth from a river;
O Maheśānī! in the absence of a river, O beloved, [use] the earth of a small stream.
The characteristics of a river and a small stream are also [to be understood].
O Goddess! that which originates from a mountain is declared by the name "River" (nadī). O Maheśāni! O Beloved! a river distinct from this is called "Minor" (kṣudrā).
And the clay of a spring, O Queen of Gods, bestows prosperity.

And likewise, O Maheśānī, when all else is absent, one may take earth from a cow’s footprint; or rather, O Parameśānī, wherever the mind finds delight. Thus indeed, they arise in various forms, bestowing manifold happiness.
O beloved! Having fashioned an earthen liṅga that is well-formed, beautiful, delightful, always free from grit, and accompanied by the *kuṇḍalī*,
he who [worships] that liṅga, O Supreme Goddess, is Rudra, the Supreme Lord himself.
She who encircles Kuṇḍalinī is that Goddess, the Supreme Sovereign.
O Goddess! By the worship of Śiva, both the Goddess and the God are worshipped. O Goddess! By the worship of one, there is indeed the complete worship of both.
In the second chapter of the Liṅgārccanatantre.

But the clay, O Supreme Goddess! O Beautiful One, [is distinguished] by the distinction of caste—by the distinction of caste, that is, by the distinction of castes such as the Brāhmaṇa and so forth. This distinction of caste has been explained previously.
Having deliberated with the *mātṛkā* mantras in both direct and reverse order, O Supreme Goddess! having recited the mantra ten times, O Sovereign Lady!
and having indeed prayed to the clay, O Fair-faced One!
O Goddess, composed of all powers! O Mṛttikā! O Sovereign of the thirty deities!
Having fashioned this earthen liṅga, I perform the worship of Śiva;
for in you, O Sovereign, both desire and righteousness reside within that very process.
O Goddess, bestower of the four aims of life! O Goddess adorned with various jewels!
O Supreme Sovereign! Without you, whence can there be liberation? Whence can there be happiness? O Mistress of the Gods! Neither wealth nor desire arises without you.
"Oṃ hrīṃ! O Earth, remover of evil deeds! Hrīṃ oṃ!"—having recited this mantra, O beloved, one should take up the earth.
Or, O lady of pure smiles, one may take it while reciting "Oṃ, salutation to Hara."

O Supreme Goddess! If one should take up the clay out of ignorance, his worship of the earthen liṅga becomes fruitless. O Beloved! The fashioning [of the liṅga] should be performed with the Mātṛkā-mantras, ending with "Salutation to Maheśvara."
Having recited the Mātṛkā-mantra, O Śūlaprāṇa!
and thereafter having recited "Be well-established," and then the Mātṛkā once more,
one should enjoin the vital breath (*prāṇa*) into the earthen Śiva-liṅga, O Goddess!
Then, one should infuse the vital breaths by means of the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra.
Also in the fifth chapter of the Toḍalatantra:
Listen, O Goddess! I shall describe the worship of Śiva performed with earth.
First, O Goddess, one whose mind is focused on no other should gratify the Guru and the God;
then, the wise one should take earth while reciting "Oṃ, salutation to Hara."
Having performed a prostration with great effort to Maheśvara,
and having uttered "O Trident-bearer!
Be well-established here," one should perform the *jīvanyāsa* (infusion of life) with this mantra, O Goddess.
The syllable *ha* joined with the *bindu* and endowed with the long vowel constitutes the six limbs.
In the *Liṅgārcanatantra*.
O Great Goddess! The purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) has first been proclaimed. Thereafter, one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkās (mātṛkānyāsa) with supreme effort.
Then, O lady of pure smiles, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should meditate upon Śiva.
As for meditation, it is [described] in the Toḍalatantra.
I shall describe his meditation; listen, O well-composed one!
One should constantly meditate upon Maheśa, who resembles a mountain of silver, adorned with the beautiful moon, and whose limbs are radiant with jeweled ornaments.
Holding an axe, a deer, a boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands,
