serene, seated upon a lotus, praised on all sides by hosts of immortals, clad in a tiger skin, the primordial source of the universe,
the seed of the universe, the remover of all fears, five-faced and three-eyed.
"Whose limbs are radiant with a jewel-ornament" means one whose limbs are brilliant because of the jewel-ornament, that is, the attire consisting of jewels;
"wearing a tiger-skin" means wearing— that is, covering oneself with— the skin of a tiger.
The meaning is: that which covers it.
Placing a flower upon one’s head, one should perform worship with mental offerings. Again meditating, O Maheśānī, and placing the flower on the head,
one should utter "Pinākadhṛk" and say "ihāvaha" twice.
"Stay here! Then [place] the pair; bring the two near here!
O Rudra, being present here, then utter your own name!
Having recited this up to the point of the worship, then I shall indeed perform it."
And for the bath, one should offer salutation to Paśupati with the suffix -ṅe.

O Goddess! The worship mantra is that which begins with the Veda; the Brahmin who recites it is the best of practitioners. "The beginning of the Veda" is the *praṇava* (Om). O Maheśānī! This is the water for the feet (*pādya*), [accompanied by] the six-syllabled mantra.
Then,
having uttered the salutation, the wise one should offer everything.
The measure of the six syllables, however, is found in that very same place.
Having extracted Nakulīśa, adorned with the vowel *manu* (the letter *u*), and joined with the *bindu*,
*nāda*, and *kalā*, one obtains Maheśvara known as Prasāda.
Here, Nakulī is the letter *ha*.
The vowel *au* is the sound of humans.
I have declared the majesty of this mantra in the Ūrdhvāmnāya:
having extracted the word of salutation (*namaskāra*), it is joined with the letter *va* (the last of the labials) and endowed with the eye (*i*).
The *vāruṇa* [syllable] is the face-circle, and *vāyu* is joined with the forehead.
O Goddess, when this five-syllabled mantra begins with the *praṇava*, it then becomes a six-syllabled mantra that bestows the fruits of the five traditions (*pañcāmnāya*).
The word *namaskāra* has the nature of the word *namaḥ*. The letter *śa* is at the end.
"The eye" refers to the right eye because it is encountered first; by that, the vowel *i* is meant.
The letter *ya* belongs to Varuṇa;
the letter *ā* is the opening of the mouth;
the letter *ya* is longevity; and the letter *a* is the forehead.
Having extracted the one called Prasāda for Arddhanārīśvara,
and having again extracted the Prasāda— the mantra that is most secret—
thus, O Daughter of the Mountain, my form is of many diverse kinds.

Having worshipped [the primary deity], O Maheśānī, one should worship the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti): Sarva, Bhava, Rudra, Ugra, Bhīma, Paśupati, Mahādeva, and Īśāna; you should diligently append the suffix "ṅe" (dative case) to each.
The best of practitioners should worship the earth, water, fire, air, and space,
as well as the sacrificer, Soma, and the Sun, together with their personified forms,
everywhere adding the dative suffix -ṅe to each name.

One should worship with the mantra beginning with *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*, proceeding in a counter-clockwise direction. These eight forms of Śiva are to be worshipped in order starting from the east and ending in the southeast; one should worship them upon the altar, and worship Śiva in the *liṅga*.
Then one should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times, or one hundred times:
"Oṃ! You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us.
O Lord, may success be mine!"
"By your grace, while you remain present;
then, having taken up the hymn of praise, one should recite it and offer it.
Then, having played a wind instrument, the wise person should perform the eight-limbed prostration."
O Mahādeva! One should dismiss [the deity] with the words, "Forgive me," using the mantra of withdrawal (saṃhāra).
Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the Sūtra, which is supremely secret:
Hara, Maheśvara, Śūlapāṇi, and Pinākadhṛk.

O Goddess! The best of practitioners should then worship the eight forms (aṣṭamūrti) in sequence as Paśupati, Śiva, and Mahādeva. Thereafter, O Maheśānī, he should perform the recitation (japa), and after that, the instrumental music (mukhavādya).
Also in the *Mantratantraprakāśa*: (p. 642)
The fetching of clay, the kneading, the consecration, as well as meditation,
the installation, the worship, and the dismissal— in this sequence [the deities are] Hara,
Maheśvara, Śūlapāṇi, and Pinākadhṛk.

Paśupati, Śiva, and Mahādeva are the names [of the faces] in order. One should not occupy the east in front of Śambhu, nor the north which is occupied by Śakti, nor the west since it is the back; therefore, one should resort to the south.
In another tantra:
Śarva, Bhava, Rudra, as well as Ugra and Bhīma,
Paśupati, Śiva, and Īśāna— these are the ones proclaimed.
Likewise, earth, water, fire, air, and space.
The sacrificer, Soma, and the Sun—these are the eight forms (mūrtis).
On the sacrificial altar (vedi), those eight forms are to be worshipped in counter-clockwise order.
The sacrificer is the worshipper, which is to say, the Self (ātman); thus it is stated in the *Mahimnaḥ Stava*: "O You! (tvam u).
"The earth is you, and the self is you"—
thus it was said by Puṣpadanta.
Having worshipped on the altar in counter-clockwise order, one should worship the eight forms.
Likewise.
These eight forms of Śiva, beginning from the east and ending with the southeast (āgneya) in successive order, are to be worshipped; one should worship Śiva upon the pedestal (vedī) or in the liṅga.
In the Toḍala-mantra.
If one is intent upon the initiation of power (śaktidīkṣā), nothing other than this should be performed;
for by practicing what is forbidden, O Goddess, a man becomes a partaker of sin. O Maheśānī, if one performs worship and so forth with deficiency or excess, [the same result follows].

Both that guru and his disciple incur the sin of killing Śiva, O Maheśānī! If there should be even one syllable more or less than the prescribed number of letters, O Maheśānī! the sin of killing a Brahmin (brahmahatyā) shall be incurred.
Therefore, O Mistress of the Gods, he is truly, truly the most wicked!
Having first performed worship in this manner, one should thereafter worship others;
having first worshipped Śiva, the worship of Śakti follows after that.
Or else, if all [substances] were like the water of the Gaṅgā, they would not be like urine.
Therefore, O Great Goddess! one should first worship the Liṅga;
as stated in the ninth chapter of the *Liṅgārcana-tantra*.
O beloved! Having worshipped the earthen linga with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, O Goddess,
then whatever flowers and sandalwood are given at the five faces,
as well as the three kinds of delightful food offerings— whether fragrant or devoid of fragrance— [all these are accepted].
O Goddess! Bilva leaves, kahlāra, tagara, mallikā, mālatī, yūthikā, and the enchanting karavīra; O Beloved! Padma, ketakī, kunda, and likewise āmalakī—[these are to be offered].

Having offered the kumuda, the kokanada, and all flowers born of the forest, as well as dūrvā grass and tulasī, and having worshipped the earthen image— O Pārvatī! whatever other flowers there may be, such as the dhustūra and so forth—

O Goddess of the gods! O Supreme Sovereign, Pārvatī! There is no flower equal to the *dhustūra* in my knowledge; the fruit that is obtained from the gift of ten million cows, O Parameśvarī, is attained through the offering of the *dhustūra*.
O Goddess of gods! having placed all those various flowers that have been manifested within the cosmic egg upon the earthen [liṅga],...

Although flowers have already been mentioned in the section on materials (*arthakāṇḍa*), they are written here again for the purpose of showing exceptions (*pratiprasava*) regarding prohibited flowers; thus, there is no redundancy.
O beloved! Whatever incenses, various lamps, and other ritual offerings there may be, [should be presented] according to the prescribed method.
In the tenth chapter.
Likewise, having placed the leaf of Vijayā upon the ground and having offered the leaf of Vijayā, one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The optional worship of the Liṅga is described in the twelfth chapter:
"O Goddess! having worshipped the earthen Hara according to the previously mentioned procedure, O Maheśānī, [one should worship Him] in one's own home, fashioned according to one's own capacity."
The phrase "by her own power" means by her own wife;
the word "and" (ca) implies that it was constructed by others as well, such as those related to her own household.
Having worshipped the earthly Śiva with the sixteen types of offerings,
one should thus worship Śiva with great devotion for the duration of a year.
After that, O lady of pure smiles, the secret [practice] should be performed month by month.
O fair-faced one! Having worshipped the Liṅga for as many days as there are [in the vow], O Supreme Goddess! O Maheśvarī! first taking that Liṅga there, O Beloved!
one should go at midnight to a Bilva tree.
On the new moon day, the fourteenth day, and especially on the full moon day—
on Tuesday, Saturday, or even Monday, O Pārvatī!—
one should worship with great effort while remaining naked, O Maheśvarī!
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship with thousands of bilva leaves;
O Great Goddess, the bilva leaf should be free from defects such as insects,
tender, sweet, and accompanied by three leaves, O Beloved!
O Goddess! One should not perform worship without the bilva leaf.
O Goddess! One should worship as before, according to the prescribed ritual;
thereafter, O Maheśānī!
Having carefully recited the mantra,
O Goddess, one should offer a bilva leaf individually for each [deity] separately. O fair-faced one, having purified the bilva leaf according to the prescribed rule!
He who, with a serene mind, performs this for a full year,
directing his mental focus toward his purpose, shall quickly attain his desire and become like Gaṇeśa himself.
Thereafter, O Maheśānī! having dug a pit in that spot and placed the liṅga therein, one should indeed mutter [mantras] at each respective place;
then, having offered salutations, O Maheśānī!, one should dismiss it with the words, "Forgive me."
O Supreme Goddess!
He who, with a serene mind, offers himself and practices this secret, he alone is the illustrious Sadāśiva.

The daily worship of the *liṅga* is also prescribed in that very place: "O Supreme Goddess! O Beloved! For as long as one lives upon this earth, one should worship with supreme devotion the *liṅga* which consists of Brahman."
In the Mātṛkābhedatantra, in the twelfth chapter.
Indeed, there is no consideration of purity or impurity in the worship of that Śiva;
by whatever means one may worship with bilva leaves,
that man, endowed with all perfections, is indeed Śiva himself.
Whatever deities exist within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) and whatever divine beings exist outside of it,
they all attain satisfaction solely through the worship of Śiva.
Now, the fruit of substances offered to Śiva:
In that very same place.
O Girijā, if one were to offer as an oblation even water measured by the tip of a blade of kusha grass,
that water would indeed truly become equal to the ocean;
and by placing it upon the linga, even a flower becomes like Mount Meru.
O Goddess, by the gift of whatever food remains at the top of the *liṅga*,
one obtains the fruit of gifting the entire earth; likewise,
he who worships the *śivaliṅga* even with a single blade of *dūrvā* grass [attains the same].
One shall obtain the fruit of offering arghya at the head of Sarvadeva;
if one brings ordinary water and bathes Maheśvara,
one becomes a partaker of the fruit of bathing at thirty-five million sacred fords (tīrthas).
Now follows the pacification of misfortune (riṣṭa-śānti).
From the Vīramitrodaya and the Pārāśaramādhavīya.
The man who performs an ablution for Śiva with water from a thousand pitchers,
according to the rules and with mantras, shall become long-lived.
The fruit of worshipping a single *śivaliṅga* for one day is also described in that very same place.
Whoever should give a hundred thousand milch cows to one who has mastered the Vedas,
the merit of worshipping the Liṅga for a single day is greater than that;
his fruit is superior even to the Aśvamedha sacrifice— it is not otherwise.
The specific manner of perpetual worship of the *liṅga* is described in the *Matsyasūkta*.
One should bathe the Liṅga with ghee and anoint it with sandalwood paste;
having bathed it with saffron,
one should then worship it with a pair of white garments as well as auspicious pearls.
With yakṣakardama incense, with milk and milk-rice (pāyasa),
with a wick made from lotus fiber, or likewise with a ghee lamp—
this worship, entirely white in color, shall bestow the fruit of all desires.
Even for one who is without a sacred fire, the status of being "one who maintains the fire" (sāgnika) is attained through the worship of the linga.
As it has been said in the Mātṛkābhedatantra:
One should place flowers, incense, water, and ritual substances upon the *liṅga*.
Within Śiva resides the great fire, and he is proclaimed to be Rudra. Whatever one casts upon Rudra, that very thing is reduced to ashes.
O Maheśānī! Direct oblation arises from the worship of Śiva;
through the worship of Śiva, a mortal becomes the Lord of the Great Sacrifice.

The *Liṅgārccanatantro* states in its twelfth chapter that a substance placed upon the *liṅga* is not to be taken [by hand]: [The *Liṅgārccanatantro* states in its twelfth chapter that a substance placed upon the *liṅga* is not to be taken.]

O Maheśānī! Whatever is offered to Śiva, the Supreme Self, O Parameśānī! all that becomes identical with Him at that very moment. Indeed, whatever article of worship one should present upon the Liṅga—
O Maheśānī! O Parameśvarī! That remains of the offering (nirmālya) is not to be accepted.
And the knowledge of the cause of its ungraspability is in the thirteenth chapter.
O Mahādeva! That *nirmālya* of yours is very difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to obtain;
how then, O wielder of yoga, do you say that your *nirmālya* is not to be accepted?
Thus follows the speech of the Lord immediately after the question of the Goddess.
O Parameśvarī! That which is situated in the middle position is the face;
it is Śyāmala, and that is Īśāna, always above, O lady of pure smiles! O Maheśānī! The face above, O lady of beautiful countenance, is composed of radiant light.
O Goddess! During the churning of the ocean of milk, a great poison emerged.
Having introduced [the topic] with these and other such words.
Then, O Supreme Goddess! having taken that poison into the palm of her hand;
then, O Dear One! having drunk that poison from the dark face of the Goddess;
from that time forward, O Queen of Gods! her mouth has always been ablaze with flames.
But having become poison in the throat, O passionate woman, it remains there forever!
In the fourteenth chapter.
O Maheśānī! The knowledge of Īśāna is extremely difficult to attain;
by the mere hearing of it, one obtains the fruit of worshipping Śiva. O Goddess, O lady of beautiful countenance, that face of his is Īśāna, the Supreme Brahman.

O lady of excellent complexion! O Supreme Goddess! Whether it be a leaf, or a flower, or water, or indeed any other beautiful offering, O Parvati, he who offers it upon her face, O Supreme Goddess! [attains the highest state].

That offering (nirmālya) is indeed ungraspable, for it is directly composed of Brahman. O Supreme Goddess! Whoever wears this offering, O Goddess, he becomes fallen; there is truly no atonement for him.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, my *nirmālya* (remains of offerings) is ungraspable;
likewise, O beloved, having placed the offering in another pure vessel, [one should proceed].

Having performed the ritual service purified by mantra, one should present it, O lady of excellent complexion, always into the mouths of Vāmadeva and the others. O Goddess of gods! This consumption is that which brings about the satisfaction of the entire universe for me.
O Supreme Goddess! This is indeed very difficult even for Brahmā and the other gods to obtain.
Whether one is impure or pure, if one should consume the remnants [of this offering], O lady of radiant smiles, he alone is the supreme object of worship; he is the manifest Brahman itself.
O Pārvatī, he who, out of firm devotion, should take my *nirmālya*,
O beautiful one, should first offer it to Viṣṇu with the Viṣṇu-mantra. O Maheśvarī, O Queen of Gods, my *nirmālya* is to be accepted from Viṣṇu.
O Supreme Goddess! Gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, kinnaras, and others—all of them are wretched beings of petty intellect. O Queen of the Gods! How could anyone have authority over my *nirmālya*?
In the fourth chapter of the Mātṛkābhedatantra.
Caṇḍikā said:

"O Maheśvara! It has been heard in the Vedas and Purāṇas that great liberation is attained through the *kāraṇa* and the *nirmālya* of Śiva. Yet in your words, O All-pervading Lord, it is said that the *nirmālya* of Śiva is not to be accepted, and the *kāraṇa* is not to be accepted."
O Mahādeva! O bearer of yoga, how can you speak such a falsehood?
The illustrious Śaṅkara said:
Indeed, the soul wanders through eighty-four lakhs and thousands of births; thereafter, it becomes a vessel for liberation.
O Goddess worshipped by the gods! if, in the midst of this, there should arise great wisdom, [then liberation is attained].
At that very moment one attains liberation; for whom could there be further wandering?
How can he whose birth is incomplete be a vessel for liberation?
And how can he who possesses an excess of sin be a vessel for heaven?
For this very reason, O Great Goddess, I have kept this state secret:
one may attain heaven through the *nirmālya* (the remains of an offering) and achieve liberation (*nirvāṇa*) through the *sudhā* (ambrosia).
Even a Caṇḍāla, though burdened with sin, attains [merit] when he takes up the *nirmālya*.
Then one truly attains liberation, for one is of the nature of Śiva and not otherwise.
Even if one is burdened with great sins, if the causal [nectar] is drunk, liberation through knowledge occurs; this is true, for distinctions such as caste do not exist.
O Supreme Goddess! Nirvāṇa is attained through knowledge in all births;
for this very reason, O Great Sovereign, I have kept this state secret.
In the Padma Purāṇa:
One should never touch the substances, food, fruits, or water belonging to Śiva. One should not take the *nirmālya* (remnants) of Śiva; rather, one should throw it all into a well.
He who makes use of even as much as a fly’s foot of Śiva’s property [is guilty].
Out of greed and delusion, a man surely falls into hell until the end of the eon.
In the Purāṇasaṃgraha.
Śiva said:
My offerings of leaves, flowers, fruits, and water are unworthy;
yet, once they have come into contact with a Śālagrāma stone, everything attains purity. A person who has consumed such an offering should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for purification.
Thus concludes the expiation for consuming the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
The subject of the *vāṇaliṅga* and *nirmālya* in the dialogue between Śiva and Nārada.
In the case of a Bāṇaliṅga, there is no impurity, nor is there any requirement for ritual cleansing of the offerings (nirmālya).
Everything offered to Bāṇa is to be accepted with devotion by devotees, and not otherwise.
This consideration regarding what is acceptable or unacceptable does not exist in the case of a Bāṇaliṅga.
The water and the leaf offered to Him should be accepted under the designation of *prasāda*;
likewise, the acceptability of the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) from Svayambhū and other such deities is established in that very same source.
In the case of a self-manifested (svayambhū) Liṅga made of bamboo, situated under a moonstone or an Indra-tree,
it should be known that by consuming the food offerings (naivedya) of Śambhu there, one gains merit equal to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Furthermore, the ritual arrangement of the remains of the offering (nirmālya) has been described in the Siddhāntaśekhara.
Having set aside land, gold, cows, gems, copper, silver, garments, and so forth, one should offer the remaining remains of the offering (nirmālya) to Caṇḍeśa.
By this, it follows that there is a fault in taking the garments and other items offered to the Liṅga.
By the statement "one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa," it is indicated that what has been offered to Caṇḍeśa must not be consumed.
[This applies except] in the case of a linga originating from a Śālagrāma stone, a jyotirliṅga, or a self-manifested (svayambhū) linga.
Likewise, those immortals [who worship] at the Indraliṅga established by the Siddhas—
at the Indraliṅga, that is, at a liṅga made of a special sapphire (indranīlamaṇi).
The same kind of explanation applies here as well to the phrase "situated upon the moon-gem king" mentioned previously.
The words of Śambhu addressed to Hanumān.
When a self-manifested (svayambhūta) Bāṇaliṅga is present, with the form of the moon situated in the heart,
the consumption of Śambhu’s food offering (naivedya) should be known as equal to the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
[This applies] to a self-manifested liṅga, a Bāṇa-liṅga, and a liṅga fashioned from mercury (rasa).
In that which is established as *siddha*, there can be no authority for *caṇḍa*.
Wherever there is authority for *caṇḍa*, that must not be eaten by human beings;
but where there is no authority for *caṇḍa*, that may be eaten with devotion.
Thus, from the words of Śiva in the *Pañcapuruṣārthaprabodha*:
"Of what use is initiation, of what use is austerity, of what use is meditation, or of what use is sacrifice?
Listen, O Goddess, O lady of beautiful hips! If my devotee is fed..."
The meaning is that "my devotee" refers to one who offers [food] to me.

Furthermore, since even the *vāṇa-liṅga* and other such forms fall under the category of *naivedya* (offered food), the author— who asserts that there is no fault in Śambhu’s consuming the *naivedya* from *vāṇa-liṅgas* and the like— [implies this].
Therefore, for that reason, the wearing of *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) is permitted;
however, the wearing of the sacred water (*tīrtha*) from Śrī Viśvanātha and other such waters must certainly be performed.
Thus it is stated in the Kāśī-khaṇḍa of the Skanda Purāṇa:
Beginning with the statement, "O Viśveśa, the holding of water upon the head [is for] another birth," it continues:
"Having bathed [the deity] according to the prescribed rite, whoever drinks three times the water used for bathing the Liṅga, his threefold sin is quickly destroyed here in this world."
O Pot-born One! For him who performs a head-ablution with the waters used for worshipping the excellent Liṅga, the fruit of bathing in the Gaṅgā arises.
Likewise, in the narrative of Vāṇeśvara.
For those devoted followers who possess faith, even in the face of great calamity,
there is truly no other remedy whatsoever except for the water from the feet of the Lord of Ishvara.
Those diseases of embodied beings, whether external or internal, which are known to be exceedingly difficult to endure—
They perish simply by the touch of the water of the Lord; it cannot be otherwise.
In rites such as pacification (śāntika) and others, the worship of the Śiva-linga is prescribed in the Kukkuṭeśvara-tantra.
Pārvatī said:
O God of gods! O Mahādeva! O Supreme Lord! O Ancient One! O Supreme Sovereign!
By Your grace, O Mahādeva, I have heard many kinds of teachings regarding the Dināstra, the Paramāstra, and the Kṛtyāstra.
Now I wish to hear about the weapon called Pāśupata;
please tell me of it, if you have any affection for me.
Sadāśiva said:
"Excellent, O Great Goddess, you who act for the benefit of all living beings!
Out of affection for you, I shall explain that most wonderful weapon— a Yoga equal to my own life-breath, difficult even for the gods to obtain."
This must be guarded with great effort; I swear it to you again and again.
I shall explain all of this—the measurement of the *liṅga*, the measurement of the materials, the mode of worship, and the procedure for recitation—listen, O lotus-faced one!
One should have an excellent liṅga fashioned from one hundred *tolakas* of fine clay.
For rites of subjugation (*vaśya*), one should bathe it with ghee or honey;
O Goddess, for pacification (*śānti*) and also for the conquest of death (*mṛtyuñjaya*), one should bathe it with milk.
For attraction, use honey; for cruel rites, use ashes.
O Goddess of the Suras, this substance is prescribed at a measure of one hundred *tolakas*; that same measure applies to the powdered *saṃvid* and the food offering (*naivedya*).

One should offer one hundred and eight bilva leaves and flowers for rites such as pacification (śāntika). For rites of subjugation (abhicāraka), one should use droṇa flowers and varvarā; likewise, for paralyzing (stambhana) and deluding (mohana), one should use dhustūra and the flower called kanaka.

O Goddess! For the purpose of inciting enmity and eradication, one should worship either the *javā* or the *aparājitā* flower with a spirit of devotion, worshipping each individual *liṅga* in sequence starting from the fourteenth day until the next fourteenth day.
One should perform the recitation (japa) one thousand and eight times every day;
in seven days, seven lingas [are consecrated], or in five days, five.
According to the procedure of Caṇḍogra, the recitation, worship, and other rites are prescribed.
O Dear One! For rites of pacification (śāntika), one should perform recitation and worship with the Vaṭuka mantra, or the Mañjughoṣa mantra, or the Tryambaka mantra;
one should carry out the worship and recitation according to the specific procedure prescribed for each respective rite.
O Goddess! when the destruction of one's lineage occurs, when the extinction of the family is at hand, when the end of life has arrived,
when great fear has arisen, or when all manner of malevolent spells are employed—
one should diligently worship one hundred and eight lingas.
One should sprinkle the ends of the ears with streams from a cascade of milk;
or, at the beginning of the Atirudra ritual and other such rites,
one should please Śiva, O Goddess, with the Rudrādhyāya or with the Nīlakaṇṭha hymn.
One should also give garments, ornaments, decorations, and so forth, according to one's means;
O Goddess, this bestows all desires and grants all prosperity. O Goddess, there exists nothing superior to this in the three worlds.
Thus, O Goddess, I have related to you this weapon called Pāśupata;
it must never be spoken of to just anyone, nor should it ever be disclosed.

One should feed the Brahmins according to one's ability, being humble with devotion and composed in mind; [this applies] to the periods other than the Kali age, because that [feeding] is prohibited during the Kali age by a statement from the *Kālīvilāsatantra*: "By Nīlakaṇṭha... and so forth.
Now, the Hymn to Śiva: Oṃ! O Omniscient One! Bestower of knowledge and realization! O Great Soul!
Salutations to You, Lord of all gods, who are devoted to the welfare of all beings!
O you who are endowed with infinite splendor! O you who abide upon the infinite throne!
O supreme lord, whose enjoyment is the ultimate splendor! Homage be to you!
O you who transcend that which is higher than the highest! O creator of the origin and maintenance [of the world]!
O means for accomplishing all goals! O Lord of the Universe! Homage be to You!
O You whose enjoyment is stainless in all matters! O destroyer of all diseases!
O Lord of Yogis, Mahāyogis, and supreme Yogis! Homage be to You!
Having fashioned a *liṅga* and performed its installation, and having meditated upon the Lord Sadāśiva and worshipped Him according to the prescribed rite, one should recite this hymn of praise.
The man who always hears this highly meritorious *Liṅgastava* [attains great merit].
One is not reborn in saṃsāra and attains the eternal state;
therefore, with every effort, one should listen to this excellent instruction.
Freed from the cloak of evil, one attains the supreme state.
Thus ends the hymn to the Liṅga as spoken in the Bhaviṣya Purāṇa.
Now, the armor-mantra.
In the Rudrajāmala:
Bhairava said:

O Goddess! I shall speak this auspicious armor (*kavaca*) which protects life, adorned by the gods, for the sake of Mahādeva’s protection day and night. Om; of this Śrī Mahādeva-kavaca, Vāmadeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *paṅkti* meter is the meter (*chanda*), and *hasau* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The deity is Nidhi; the application is for all ritual accomplishments (*sarvasādhana*).
May Rudra protect me from the front, and may Śaṅkara protect me from behind.
May Kapardin protect my right side, and likewise Hara my left side.
May Śiva protect my head; may Nīlalohita protect my forehead; may the Eyeless One (Netryakṣara) protect my eye; may Maheśvara protect the pair of my arms;
and may Mahādeva protect my heart, as well as Īśvara protect my belly.
May Maheśvara protect my navel, belly, and waist;
may Hara, the Lord of Beings, protect my feet and all my limbs.
May he protect [me with] the noose, the trident, the divine weapon, the sword, and the thunderbolt as well.
I pay homage to the Lord of Beings; O Lord of the Universe, protect me! Save me from sins and from hells, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees!
Save me also from birth, death, old age, disease, desire, and anger, O Lord!
O Mahādeva! O Lord of the Thirty-three! Protect me from greed and delusion!
You are my refuge, you are my intellect, you are my prosperity, and you are my ultimate goal.
May my devotion to you be firm through body, mind, and speech.
This Rudraka-armor, which destroys sin through recitation,
was proclaimed by Bhairava through the grace of Mahādeva.
For such a person, no sin exists in the body, nor does any fear exist for them.
One obtains happiness, health, and the increase of sons and longevity;
one desiring a son obtains sons, and one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
one desiring knowledge obtains knowledge, and one desiring liberation obtains liberation itself.
The sick person is freed from disease, and the bound is released from bondage;
even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin perish merely by reciting this.
Thus ends the Śrīśivakavaca in the Rudrajāmala.
Now, the majesty of the bilva tree and others.
In the *Yoginītantra*, in the first section, the fifth chapter.
O Maheśānī! Know that the bilva root extends sixteen cubits on all sides;
O beautiful one, know its leaf to be the very form of my matted locks.
O lady of lovely countenance, its three petals are like the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
Know, O lotus-eyed one, that all the branches are all the scriptures!
The bilva tree is equal to the wish-fulfilling kalpa-vṛkṣa, being of the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
the Mahālakṣmī tree was born on the Śrīśaila mountain.
The Goddess said:
How did that wife of Viṣṇu become a bilva tree?
She was the embodiment of light, the destroyer of pride, and was constantly entreated by Brahmā and the other gods.
Through my grace in that matter, her speech became dear to everyone.
Sarasvatī was always eternally very dear to Viṣṇu; such affection as that did not arise for Lakṣmī from Keśava either. Thinking thus, Lakṣmī went to the temple of Śrīśaila.
Having reached my *liṅga* in solitude, she performed most rigorous penance;
yet, O Supreme Goddess, if even so you did not show compassion toward me,
then that virtuous one, who is dear to the *liṅga*, remained there in the form of a tree.
O Great Goddess! She worshipped [him] constantly with her own leaves and flowers for ten million years (koṭivarṣa). Then my grace was bestowed upon her;
by that very grace, she came to reside within the chest of Viṣṇu.
O Supreme Goddess! Brahmins are indeed always under my control;
for that reason, O Goddess, those who are devoted to me and equal to me, O Śivā, should always worship me in that form, being dear to the Heart.

Therefore, O Goddess, I remain day and night taking refuge in that tree. O Supreme Sovereign, there is no doubt that the Śrīvṛkṣa is always composed of all holy fords (tīrthas) and composed of all gods.
Whoever worships with its fruits, its flowers, or its leaves,
or even with sandalwood made from its wood— he is my devotee, he is dear to me;
he who, out of devotion, wears that sandalwood upon his forehead.
Filled with joy, she bowed to that body with the thought that it was Śiva;
therefore, O Goddess, no one wears that sandalwood paste,
nor indeed should anyone ever wear its leaves or its flowers.
O Maheśānī! That man who gives up his life at the root of the bilva tree truly becomes the very body of Rudra, even if he is burdened by tens of millions of sins.
In the tenth chapter of the *Puraścaraṇarasollāsa*.
O Goddess, the Bilva tree is indeed the Lord Śaṅkara himself;
if a wise person stands at the foot of a Bilva tree and gives up his life,
he attains liberation at that very moment— what need has he for ten million holy places?
Wherever the gods, beginning with Brahmā, reside for the sake of their power—
even if the ground beneath a bilva tree is filled with excrement and the like—
that very spot is the sacred field of Śaṅkara and is eternally composed of all holy pilgrimage sites.
The reality is always composed of all sacred seats (pīṭhas) and consists of all the gods.
One should not abandon the field of Śaṅkara, nor should one abandon the Gaṅgā, O beloved!
And if there is a bilva tree nearby, O lovely-limbed one, O dear one!
That place is indeed equal to the city of Kāśī; if one should give up one's life there, what need has one for Koṭitīrtha, O beloved, and what need for residence in Kāśī?
Now follows the construction of the altar at the foot of the Bilva tree.
In that very same Middle Section, in the twelfth chapter.
Having constructed the altar (vedikā), preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (svastivācana),

one should proceed from the northeast (īśāna) to the southeast (agnikoṇa), and from there enter the southwest (rākṣasa). From the southwest to the northwest (vāyukoṇa), and from the northwest to the northeast (maheśaka).
One should take a level plot of ground in the four directions for the purpose of yoga.
O Dear One! It should be eight cubits in length and likewise in width;
it should have a beautifully adorned altar (vedikā) one span high.

Above that, however, one should know the Mahāvedī to be sixteen cubits on all sides; that is the place of worship. O Dear One, this rule applies everywhere—in the cremation grounds and so forth—and its measurement is likewise the same there.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a cremation ground, at the foot of an aśvattha tree in the wilderness,
on a riverbank, in the womb of a deity, in the womb of the Gaṅgā, at a crossroads,
in a thicket, on a mountain, or in a garden filled with flowers.
In a temple of Śiva, in an empty house, or in one's own home;
in the house of a courtesan, in a place of creepers, in a cow-pen, or in any other such place.
Thus it is said; and in the Rudrajāmala as well, the measurement of the pedestal (vedikā) is stated as follows:
One who knows the ritual procedure should construct an altar at the root of an *aśvattha* or *bilva* tree;
facing the northern direction, the wise practitioner should fashion the altar. The laying of the cord should take place in the northeast, and the planting of the pillars in the southeast.
Then, one should have the ninefold sacrificial site prepared as before;
having laid out the four lines, one must not make them either too short or too long.
Indeed, the extent of the site and its height should be exactly equal.
One should make the length exactly eight cubits;
indeed, excluding the root-length, eight cubits are desired here. One should construct a well-characterized altar above, measuring one span in height.

The knower of the ritual (tantravid) should construct an altar in the center measuring four cubits in length; all else, including the laying of the lines and the planting of the pillars, is to be done exactly as before. Likewise, the length and breadth should each be four times the length of the practitioner’s own hand.
In the same manner, the excellent practitioner should leave a space of one cubit.
Now, the procedure for the installation of the five banyan trees (*pañcavaṭī*) is written here as a relevant digression.
And likewise in the Skanda Purāṇa:
The aśvattha, the bilva tree, the vaṭa, the dhātrī, and the aśoka—
these are called the "five vaṭīs," and one should place them in the five directions.
One should place the aśvattha in the east and the bilva in the northern part.

O Goddess of the Suras! For the sake of ascetic practice, one should place a banyan tree to the west, a dhātrī tree likewise to the south, and an aśoka tree in the direction of Agni (the southeast). In the center, there should be a beautiful and most enchanting altar measuring four cubits.
O Śivā, one should perform its consecration after five years have passed;
it bestows infinite fruit and grants the rewards of ascetic penance.
This is called Pañcavaṭī; now hear about Bṛhatpañcavaṭī.
One should plant a *vilva* tree in the center and four trees in the four directions;
one should plant four *vaṭa* trees at the four corners,
and twenty-five *aśoka* trees arranged in a circular shape.

O Supreme Goddess! One should plant a single *āmalaka* tree in each of the cardinal and intermediate directions; and with a *aśvattha* tree in each of the four quarters, there shall be the great *pañcavaṭī*.
O Maheśānī! He who performs this becomes equal to Indra himself.
In this world there is the accomplishment of mantras, and in the next world, the supreme goal.
Thus are the scriptural statements cited in the Vrata-khaṇḍa of Hemādri.
Now, the majesty of the bilva leaf.
In the sixteenth chapter of the Matsya-sūkta.
The reality of the bilva leaf is the supreme, imperishable state;
its leaf is divine and captivating, eternally endowed with the fifty principles and consisting of the four aims of human life— Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Pitāmaha.
O Goddess of the gods! A leaf consisting of the four aims—bestowing dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—and the bilva leaf cannot be fully described.
O Pārvatī! There is no leaf equal to the three-leafed bilva leaf.
O Maheśānī! Your three matted locks are eternally composed of all the *tattvas*:
the *ātmatattva*, O Maheśānī, the *vidyātattva* which follows it, and the *paratattva*, O Maheśānī, which is most secret and enchanting.
Likewise.
O Maheśānī! O beloved! The bilva leaf, the karavīra flower, and likewise the aparājitā flower are difficult to obtain for the worship of Śiva;
yet, by using them in the worship of Śakti, one obtains the fruit of ten million worships.
O Goddess of the Gods! The greatness of the fruit that a man obtains by offering these flowers cannot even be described. Brahmā dwells in their midst, and Janārdana resides at their base.
Among these Rudra dwells, and all the gods are situated upon its base;
O Goddess Pārvatī, the bilva leaf is composed entirely of light.
In the fifth chapter.
O Maheśānī! The bilva leaf consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
O Goddess! it possesses the nature of the three qualities (guṇas), has three leaves, and grants all desires.
In the Yoginītantra.
The greatness of the bilva leaf is difficult even for the gods to attain.
Whoever offers a bilva leaf to Śivā and to Śaṅkara,
having become equal to Sadāśiva, shall go to the abode of Brahmā.
Regarding the specific details for the offering of bilva leaves during the worship of Śiva, they are found in the Trivikrama-saṃhitā as cited in the Śrī-tattvacintāmaṇi.
O Goddess, if one offers a leaf whose base has not been severed for the worship of Śaṅkara, his worship is in vain; having died, he shall attain hell.
Thus, in the twelfth chapter of the *Mātṛkābhedatantra*.
Whatever fruit a man obtains by offering a thousand golden flowers,
a hundred-thousandfold merit is gained from even a single broken bilva leaf.
And from a thousandth part of a single broken bilva leaf [is gained the merit of all other offerings].
Indeed, that fruit is not obtained even with gold equal in weight to Mount Meru;

and thus, in the Liṅgārcanatantra, there is the statement regarding the offering of three tender, sweet bilva leaves— free from defects such as insect damage— as previously written in the twelfth chapter.
For the sake of the excellence of the fruit.
Thus ends the majesty of the bilva leaf.
Now, the majesty of the rudrākṣa.
In the second chapter of the *Yogasāra*.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
"Now, O Goddess of the gods! Tell me, O Supreme Goddess, about the auspicious wearing of garlands and the majesty of the rudrākṣa.
The Holy Goddess said:
The man who devoutly wears a rudrākṣa on his crest-lock, his hands, his neck, and also his ears, shall attain the world of Śiva. One should wear a nine-faced rudrākṣa on the left arm.
Likewise, O dear one, one who is self-controlled should wear [the beads] on the right arm;
ten should be worn on the crest-lock (śikhā) and twenty-five on the neck.

Having placed five Rudrākṣas on the ears and one hundred and eight on the heart, and seven on the navel, one becomes a partaker of liberation through such wearing. O Lord! By wearing Rudrākṣas, a man attains divinity.
On the crest-tuft, there are thirty-two teeth.
Likewise.
O Lord of the Gods! One should always wear the Rudrākṣa and the Bhadrākṣa.
O mighty-armed one! Listen with diligence to the majesty of the Rudrākṣa: the single-faced Rudrākṣa is Śiva himself and removes even the sin of killing a Brahmin.
He makes that which is unassailable flow against the current and causes the obstruction of fire.
The two-faced one is Hara-Gaurī, who effects the destruction of sins such as the killing of cows.
The three-faced one is Agni, the Lord of the World, who effects the destruction of the heap of evils.

O Hara! Just as fire reduces a heap of cotton to ashes, so too does the three-faced Rudrākṣa burn away sin. Furthermore, the four-faced one is Dhātṛ (the Creator), and he removes even the killing of a human being.
The five-faced one is the fire of time (*kālāgni*), who removes the sin of approaching those who should not be approached; Guha, who is the six-faced one, directly dispels the murder of a preceptor;
and Ananta, who indeed has seven faces, always removes the sin of stealing gold.
Vināyaka shall have eight faces and is the destroyer of all falsehoods;
Bhairava shall have nine faces and is the bestower of union with Śiva;
the ten-faced one is Viṣṇu himself, the slayer of bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
Rudra with eleven faces bestows the fruits of various sacrifices;
the Sun with twelve faces bestows the fruits of all sacred fords;
Kāma with thirteen faces bestows the fruits of all desires.
Śrīkaṇṭha, who has fourteen faces, is remembered as the one who uplifts the lineage;
as it has been stated regarding the Rudrākṣa, so too has it been proclaimed regarding the Indrākṣa,
O best of gods, and its qualities have likewise been proclaimed for the Bhadrākṣa.
The ritual procedure for these has been written by our own eminent scholar, Kṛṣṇānandāgamavāgīśa, in his own work, the *Tantrasāra*; therefore, there is no need for it here.
The measurements for those [deities] ranging from one face up to fourteen faces have also been written by him;
however, that was written considering it to be Puranic, namely from the Padma Purāṇa and Skanda Purāṇa.
"Therefore, those who perceive only a partial truth doubt that there is no fixed measurement for the rudrākṣa in the tantric scriptures; hence, the measurements are written down here."
Thus ends the majesty of the rudrākṣa.
Now begins the section on consciousness.
In the first chapter of the *Samayācāra-tantra*.
The *samayas* are proclaimed as always to be kept secret among those things that must be concealed.
O Goddess, those practitioners who consume the *samayas* according to the prescribed rite,
having enjoyed [their fruits] eternally on earth, go forever to heaven.
O Goddess! O beautiful one! One should guard the *samaya* even from one's disciples.
O Goddess! Without the *samaya*, how could one accomplish the ritual acts? Without the *samaya*, worship will never result in auspiciousness.
In the seventh chapter of the *Ācārasāra-saṃvitkalpa*.
"What should always be practiced by yogins? What bestows strength and nourishment upon the Kaulas? What removes mental instability and grants the fruit of meditative absorption?
Following these questions of the Goddess, [the Lord spoke] to Indra and the other gods, beginning with the asura named Bala.
Having described the defeat of Śakra and the others, and having introduced their journey to Kailāsa and the subsequent offering of praise, [the text presents] the words of Śiva.
Listen, O Śakra, O illustrious one! I shall tell you all this.
First, hear the names known as the Trailokyavijayā.
Out of affection for you, I shall tell you all those things that are most secret:
the Trailokyavijayā, the Siddhā, the Siddhi, the Siddhimūlikā,
the Jñāna, the Saṃvit, the Saṃvidā, the Śyāmā, the Bhaṅgā, and the Rasāyanā.
She is the bestower of yoga, the Yoginī to be served, and the illuminator of the path of yoga;
she is Brahmāṇī, born from Brahman, and the giver of the bliss of Brahman;
she brings the goddess of speech under control and bestows victory upon the victorious.
The twenty-one [names] are: Samādhivaradā and Ajñānanāśinī.
There are four types according to the distinction of white, red, black, and yellow flowers:
she who has white flowers is a Brāhmaṇī, and she who has red flowers is a Kṣatriyā.
The Vaiśya woman has yellow flowers, while the Śūdra woman has red flowers.
Having diligently gathered their leaves along with the seeds,
they should be fried in ghee and ground into powder on a stone slab.
The three pungents (trikaṭu), the three myrobalans (triphalā), śṛṅgī, kuṣṭha, dhanyāka,
saindhava salt, śaṭhī, tālīśapatra, kaṭuka, nāgakeśara, the two types of yavānī, methī, and the two types of jīraka.
One should grind these ingredients in equal parts until they are coarse and dry.
Having placed them in a vessel made of gold or another precious metal before oneself, one should then perform her purification in due order by means of the four mantras.
Having placed water there, one should purify it according to the prescribed rite:
*oṃ saṃvide* and so forth.
Then, with *oṃ brahmāṇyai namaḥ svāhā*, one should purify the Kṣatriyā.
Oṃ siddhimūlakriye! Devī... [and so forth]. Aiṃ, obeisance to the Kṣatriyā, svāhā! Thereafter, one should purify the Vaiśyā. Oṃ, [the mantra] beginning with "ajñānendhana... and so forth.
*Hrīṃ vaiśyāyai namaḥ svāhā*; thereafter, one should purify the Śūdrā.
*Oṃ namasyāmi*, etc. *Klīṃ śūdrāyai namaḥ svāhā* is the mantra for the purification of the Śūdrā.
In the fifth chapter of the Mahānirvāṇatantra.
The minister, assuming the bound hero’s posture, should purify Vijayā.
In the Muṇḍamālā Tantra.

Of this mantra of Śrī Vāgvādinī: the Brahman-sage is [the seer], Gāyatrī is the meter, Vāgvādinī is the deity, Aiṃ is the seed-syllable, Klīṃ is the pin, Sauḥ is the power; its application is in recitation for my success, for the sake of pleasing Vāgvādinī.
Having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) and the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*) according to the prescribed rule,
one should then praise the *saṃvidācūrṇa* while reciting the mantra.
Likewise.
The practitioner constantly recites the mantra obtained from the mouth of the Guru.
By that very same procedure, the mantra-master should consecrate the *samaya* woman;
having performed the consecration seven times, he should contemplate the Guru as being entirely present within her.
Having offered it to the Guru, Śiva, and likewise the Goddess, one should consume it.
In the Mahānirvāṇa Tantra.
Having uttered *Tāra* (Oṃ) and *Māyā* (Hrīṃ), one should say: "O Amṛte! O Amṛtodbhave!
O Amṛtavarṣiṇi! Then, having drawn forth the nectar in two ways, one should say:
"Grant success (*siddhi*) to me [name]," and after that, [the name].
"Bring [them] under control; this is the mantra for purifying the consciousness during the pair of *ṭha*.
Having recited the root mantra seven times over the *vijaya* [flower], one should display the *āvāhanī* and other mudrās, as well as the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās."

One should satisfy the Guru in the thousand-petaled lotus according to the secret convention-mudrā; likewise, one should satisfy the Goddess three times while reciting the root mantra in the heart, followed by the Vāgbhava-bīja, the pair of Vajra-mantras, and the words "O Vāgvādini! (O Goddess of Speech!).
"O you who bring all beings under control, become firm upon the tip of my tongue!
Svāhā!"— with this mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should offer oblations into the mouth of the Kuṇḍalī,
after having proclaimed victory over Śakra and the other gods.
Aiṃ vada vada krīṃ O Vāgvādini! Be firmly established at the tip of my tongue, O you who bring all beings under control! Svāhā!
Having consecrated [the object] seven times with this mantra and having meditated upon the Guru as well, [one should proceed].
O Goddess! the practitioner of steady mind should consume the *saṃvit* (consciousness).
Or else, O Supreme Lady, he should prepare it with this mantra:
*Oṃ jaya jaya vijaya vijaya paraṃbrahmasvarūpiṇi!* (Victory, victory! Be victorious, be victorious! O you whose nature is the Supreme Brahman!)
"Bring all people under my control, *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*!
Having drunk and eaten with this [mantra], O Mistress of the Kula,
one should mutter the desired mantra seven times with the *tattvamudrā*.
But in the Ācārasāra, there is a specific distinction as follows:
Oṃ Amṛte! Amṛtodbhave! Amṛtavarṣiṇi! [then] the word *padam*. Then [say] *amṛtam ākarṣaya* twice, and after that *siddhiṃ dehi*. Then one should say *amukaṃ*, and after that *vaśam ānaya*.
This mantra is said to end in two *ṭha*s when used for the invocation of the four *kaṇas*.
One should recite the mantra for Ānandabhairava and Ānandabhairavī there:
[the syllable] ending with Śiva (Ś), Soma (U), and Mātṛkā (Ā), [followed by] the abode of Kāla (R), Bhū (L), and Varuṇa (V);
joined with the left ear (Ū), and conjoined with Vāyu (Y) and the half-moon (Anusvāra).
Then one should utter the crest-mantra (śikhā-mantra): "To Ānandabhairava.
This belongs to Ānandabhairava; listen now to [the mantra of] Ānandabhairava.
Having written the seed-syllable as before, [one should place] the cow-seal (dhenu-mudrā) and the womb-seal (yoni-mudrā) thereafter.
One should perform the binding of the directions with finger-snaps preceded by three hand-claps;
then, with a divine gaze and strikes of the heels, one should destroy the obstacles.
One should satisfy the Guru seven times within the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*) while reciting the mantra.
In one's own thousand-petaled lotus, one should offer libations with devotion three times using the *saṅketamudrā*, or even once according to one's own desire; there,
one should worship the Guru known as Para, and then the Guru who is both Para and Apara.
Right there, while recollecting the mantra, one should offer libations to Ānandabhairavī;
one should offer libations to the Goddess within the heart with the root mantra using the *tattvamudrā*,
three times or once, using [a vessel] the size of a sesame seed or a green gram.

One should utter the word *aiṃ*, then *vada vada padaṃ*, followed by *vāgvādini*! Then the word *padaṃ*, then one should say *sapta jihvāgre sthirībhava*, and then the entire phrase *sarvapadaṃ*. Having recited *sattvavaśaṅkari!* three times with *svāhā*, one should offer oblations into the mouth.
Then, one should partake of the consciousness with the divine nectar from the mouth.
In the first chapter of the *Samayācāra-tantra*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the supreme hymn of the Samayas, by hearing which that root of accomplishment, when consumed, shall become a granter of fruits.
Oṃ! O Saṃvid! O you who are born of Brahman! O daughter of Brahman! O you who are ever stainless!
Be forever pure for the sake of the satisfaction of the Bhairavas;
you are the mother and the protector of men, adorned with the circle of garments.
You are the extinguisher of the heat of worldly existence and the great treasure-house of the wise.
Oṃ! O you who make [all things] the root of accomplishment! O awakener of inferior understanding!
O subduer of kings and subjects! O trident-wielder against the throats of enemies! Oṃ! O you whose form is wisdom, the flame-fire blazing upon the fuel of ignorance!
Considering this to be an oblation to Ānanda, grant me perfect knowledge.
Now follows the meditation on Ānandamaya.

I propitiate the Sovereign of the Universe in the three worlds, who has attained the fullness of liberation and worldly enjoyment by mounting her staff, whose face is as serene as the moon, who is habituated to granting victory,
and who is the vanquisher of many enemies.
"Victory!"—thus one should address the Goddess.
Having meditated upon this Vijayā, who is known as Ānandā, one should recite her hymn:
"I salute the mother of bliss, O you whose two feet are the state of eternal joy!"

I bow to Ānandakadalī, whose form is autonomous consciousness (svacchandabodha). The effulgence of pure awareness (saṃvidullāsa) brings about great poetry, provides men with the vision of their own true purpose, and removes the abode of sin; what indeed does it not accomplish?
Between consciousness (saṃvid) and liquor (āsava), consciousness alone is more important;
when consumed, it is fragranceless and takes the form of awakening, leading to the destruction of worldly existence.
Consciousness is the goddess Śūlinī, the Victorious One (Vijayā), and the sprout of consciousness.
Vaiṣṇavī, Tulasī, Tuṅgā, Tejoraśmī, Raseśvarī, Vimarṣā, Śvetavadvaidyā, Lakṣmīdevī, Mahodarī,
Samayā, Mohinī, Siddhamūlī, and Mahodarī.
Mātulānī is the embodiment of accomplishment, the bestower of success, and Sarasvatī;
she is the speaker of speech, eternally constant, and the giver of bliss.
One should cultivate these names, which are the very root of accomplishment.
He attains supreme knowledge and finds both worldly enjoyment and liberation;
he acquires scholarship, poetic talent, and the perfection of mantra.
Thus ends the hymn of praise to Vijayā.
Now, the fruit of consuming Vijayā according to specific substances.
In the *Ācārasāra*:
With milk, water, ghee, honey, or rock salt;
or with sugar, jaggery, or even ripe plantain;
or whatever sweet substance there may be, such as ripe mango, jackfruit, and so forth.
Therefore, Vijayā should be accepted by all practitioners;
when combined with milk, Vijayā alone increases pure bliss,
bestows great luster, and wards off defects of the eyes and other ailments.
Furthermore, when combined with water, it destroys all indigestion;
with ghee, it bestows intelligence and brings the Goddess of Speech under one's control; and when fallen [into the mouth], it confers supreme and utterly pure wisdom.
One should destroy all bodily defects without exception along with honey;
one should administer great fire [digestive power] with rock salt and common salt;
furthermore, with sugar or even jaggery, it destroys colic and acid dyspepsia (amlapitta).
It pacifies diarrhea, suppresses dyspnea and cough,
and wards off the malabsorption syndrome arising from *āmavāta*. When combined with honey, it destroys all diseases.
She bestows strength and nourishment, grants a sweet voice, and illuminates the path of knowledge, discernment, courtesy, and virtuous conduct;
what more need be said here? She is solely of the nature of pure consciousness.
Likewise:
"Between consciousness (saṃvit) and liquor (āsava), consciousness alone is superior;
therefore, the best of practitioners should employ consciousness here."
Now follows the time for consuming the *saṃvit* [wine].
Whether once a day, twice a day, thrice a day, or five times a day;
whether one *tolaka*, half a *tolaka*, or two *tolakas*;
or whatever quantity—whether less or more—is used constantly.
When the measure is deficient or excessive, the corresponding result arises;
therefore, one who desires success and knows the proper proportions must act accordingly.
In the *Samayācāra-tantra*:
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, she destroys sins when consumed with devotion;
likewise, when the sun has risen, she is likewise effective when eaten at midday;
and similarly, at the time of afternoon, she accomplishes all goals when partaken according to the rules.
Especially at midnight, she bestows the fruits of one's desired objects.
O Goddess, how can one attain success without the observance of rules (samaya), even through recitation, worship, and the like?
Without them, one does not achieve perfection; rather, it leads to malevolent magic (abhicāra).
It removes untimely death for men, destroys disease and grief,
subdues wicked enemies, and delights all the worlds; indeed,
the supernatural powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest abide in the hand of one who possesses it.

Whatever misdeed has been committed through body, speech, or mind— all of that, including even the killing of a Brahmin, goes to destruction. He is Śiva, he is the one united [with Śakti], and he is likewise the ascetic who is so joined.
That very mortal dwells in heaven by whom the *samaya* has been protected;
he by whom the *samaya* has been consumed, and he by whom the *samaya* has been upheld—
he who has protected the *samaya* is indeed freed from all sins.
And having partaken of the *samaya* [substance], whatever mantra a person recites, he obtains the full fruit thereof; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one!
But without the *samaya*, O Goddess, if one recites the mantra constantly, [the result is otherwise].
He will become short-lived and will certainly provoke the wrath of the deity immediately.
In the Kubjikātantra, in the seventh chapter.
O Goddess! Without the samaya, one shall never attain success;
therefore, one should certainly receive it with great effort—of this there is no doubt.
Now, the inhalation of Vijayā-smoke, from the first chapter of the *Yogasāra*.
Alternatively, the cessation of hunger is prescribed by another method:
the knower of mantras, the lord of yoga, daily drinks the smoke of Vijayā through the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*); hunger is certainly destroyed.
I shall declare the Brahma-mantra by which the destruction of hunger occurs:
the letters *saṃ* and *va*, joined with *rtta*, followed by the Moon (*ca*), Fire (*ra*), and Earth (*bha*), each conjoined with the Bindu (*m*).
O God, Kuleśvara! having thus uttered these three seed-syllables—
By this [mantra] which is neither deficient nor redundant, the purification of the smoke of victory is performed.
Having purified it, one should drink the smoke; O Hara, no fault exists.
The mantra, however, is: *kṣrauṃ kṣrauṃ kṣrauṃ*.
In the *Yogasāra*:
Alternatively, another method for the practice of eating by morsels is prescribed:
first, one should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya); afterwards, one recites the Mātṛkā;
and thereafter, O Śaṅkara, ghee should be consumed with this mantra.
The best of practitioners should consume it with the mantra using the seed-syllable *hasau*.
Thus ends the inhalation of the Vijayā-smoke.
Thus ends the section on Vijayā.
Thus ends the third chapter, consisting of the exposition on the section concerning Śiva, within the fifth division, the Section on Devotion, of the venerable *Prāṇatoṣiṇī*.
